items.title: Colonización perceptual y experiencia educativa en comunidades sordas: una mirada decolonial
items.abstract: This article examines perceptual colonization as an educational mechanism that renders the communicative possibilities of sign languages invisible. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with deaf university students and hearing educational stakeholders in Culiacán, Sinaloa, Mexico, and the Attitudes Toward Deaf Culture Scale (25 items; n = 54), the study examines four dimensions: linguistic-cultural inferiorization, normalization of exclusionary practices, assimilationism, and bias toward oral communication models. Grounded in ecological psychology and decolonial epistemology, the concept of disaffordance is used to interpret socially shaped constraints on the perception of action possibilities. The findings show a negative correlation between familiarity with the deaf community and overall scale scores (ρ = −.48, p < .001). This exploratory result does not establish causality or demonstrate that interaction reverses these constraints. The findings raise questions about the recognition of sign languages in educational settings and suggest avenues for future research into potential processes of perceptual transformation. Implications for teacher education and inclusion policies are discussed.

items.title: ESTERILIZAÇÃO VOLUNTÁRIA PRECOCE: IMPLICAÇÕES PSICOLÓGICAS NA DECISÃO REPRODUTIVA DE JOVENS À LUZ DA LEI Nº 14.443/2022
items.abstract: A decisão pela esterilização voluntária durante a juventude envolve aspectos psicológicos, sociais e culturais que ultrapassam a escolha de um método contraceptivo definitivo. Nesse contexto, o presente estudo teve como objetivo analisar, por meio de revisão bibliográfica, os aspectos psicológicos envolvidos na decisão reprodutiva de jovens que optam pela esterilização voluntária, considerando as mudanças estabelecidas pela Lei nº 14.443/2022. A pesquisa caracteriza-se como bibliográfica, de abordagem qualitativa e caráter exploratório e descritivo, desenvolvida a partir da análise de artigos científicos, livros e documentos relacionados à temática. Os resultados da análise apontaram que a decisão pela esterilização voluntária pode estar relacionada à autonomia reprodutiva, aos projetos de vida, às experiências familiares, às condições socioeconômicas e às expectativas em relação ao futuro. Também foi possível compreender que sentimentos de ambivalência e possíveis dúvidas não representam, necessariamente, ausência de maturidade ou incapacidade de decisão. Nesse sentido, destaca-se a importância de uma atuação psicológica pautada no acolhimento, na escuta e no respeito à singularidade de cada indivíduo, sem julgamentos ou imposições. Conclui-se que a compreensão da esterilização voluntária entre jovens exige uma perspectiva ampla, que reconheça a autonomia e a diversidade das escolhas reprodutivas.

items.title: Mathematical Cognition and the Multiple-Demand System: A Critical Review and Integrative Framework
items.abstract: This review critically evaluates the claim, associated primarily with Amalric and Dehaene (2016, 2018, 2019), that high-level mathematics is supported by a distinct cortical network. I argue that the dissociation between mathematics and language is well established, but that the stronger claim of a mathematics-specific network remains empirically unresolved. The review integrates three converging literatures: (a) the multiple-demand (MD) system literature, (b) the individual-differences and dyscalculia literatures, and (c) the occupational neuroplasticity literature. It proposes an integrative framework in which mathematical cognition is understood as a distributed architecture involving domain-specific representations, domain-general control mechanisms, and interactions between them. It also specifies a critical experiment (a preregistered, factorial, expert-to-expert comparison of mathematical and formally matched logical reasoning) that would discriminate between competing accounts. The manuscript is a review article, not a primary empirical study. It contains no new data. It is intended for researchers in cognitive neuroscience, mathematical cognition, and developmental psychology.

items.title: Discrimination of ranges of closely related RNA targets using CRISPR-based detection assay developed using machine learning-based optimization
items.abstract: Abstract Early detection and identification of pathogen strains are crucial for mitigating infectious disease threats, including those posed by closely related zoonotic variants. A key limitation of current molecular detection approaches is their narrow focus on individual targets, which can delay recognition of outbreaks caused by closely related but non-identical pathogens. Here we report a two-channel CRISPR/Cas13a detection assay capable of discriminating between SARS-CoV-2 and a panel of twelve closely related zoonotic sarbecoviruses using a compact duplex assay format. Guide RNA sets with tunable specificity were designed using a two-stage machine learning pipeline: initial candidate filtering with a pre-existing RuleFit model, followed by retraining on 382 sarbecovirus-specific in vitro data points to refine the mismatch threshold from 4 to 6 mismatches for target exclusion. The optimized assay achieved proof-of-concept three-way classification of synthetic RNA targets into: (1) SARS-CoV-2, (2) the closest known near-neighbor BANAL-236, and (3) remaining zoonotic near-neighbors, with a limit of detection of 15–150 fM for synthetic RNA targets. This approach provides a practical framework for surveillance-oriented detection that identifies not only a specific pathogen but also its closest relatives, provided that system-specific validation and model retraining are included for new target systems.

items.title: Genomic diversity and structure of a thermoconforming anole recolonizing secondary forest
items.abstract: Abstract Over half of tropical forests worldwide are secondary forests recovering from disturbance. As these forests regenerate, they develop complex structures that meet the requirements for recolonization by previously extirpated fauna. While community-level patterns of fauna recolonization of tropical secondary forests are well-documented, less is known about the underlying evolutionary processes. Eco-evolutionary theory predicts that expanding populations may experience a reduction in genetic diversity due to the small number of founding individuals, a pattern largely supported by studies of biological invasions and post-glacial recolonizations. However, recolonization of recovering forests differs fundamentally: populations may remain connected to extant sources and share evolutionary history with the habitat. Therefore, if such expansions also reduce genetic diversity remains unclear. To address this gap in knowledge, we analyzed genome-wide SNP data from Anolis gundlachi , an endemic shade-specialist lizard recolonizing secondary forests in Puerto Rico, comparing adjacent forests of varying ages (10–30, 30–50, >70 yrs). We tested whether recently colonized young forests exhibit reduced genetic diversity or distinct allele frequences compared to old-growth forests. Overall, our results revealed comparable genetic diversity and structure among anole populations living in forests of varying ages. This pattern likely reflects isolation by distance, ongoing gene flow among forests, or phenotypic plasticity. This study suggest that the evolutionary dynamics of recolonization are complex and strongly influenced by local factors such as landscape connectivity, rather than following classic founder-effect scenarios.

items.title: Dynamic spatio-temporal sequential ordinal models: Application to invasive weeds
items.abstract: Abstract The multivariate sequential ordinal model is investigated for use in the Bayesian analysis of spatio-temporal ordinal data. The sequential ordinal model likelihood is equivalent to a binary model conditional on unknown regression coefficients and spatio-temporal random effects. Therefore estimation and prediction in the space-time context can proceed using the well-established dynamic generalised linear model framework. Moreover, the sequential ordinal model avoids the ordering constraints on the threshold parameters that determine the category break points required by cumulative ordinal models, and so simplifies the estimation procedure for high-dimensional space-time applications using Bayesian inference. The dynamic spatio-temporal sequential ordinal model is applied to estimate the cover-abundance of four invasive alien weed species. These weeds are observed by means of a modified Braun-Blanquet score that is commonly used in vegetation studies and constitutes ordinal data. As all four weeds are actively managed, the multivariate ordinal data are sparsely distributed in space and time with few observations recorded in high cover-abundance categories. A separable model for space-time dependence that maintains parameter interpretability in the presence of aggregated ordinal categories is therefore developed and applied to each species of interest. The dynamic spatio-temporal sequential ordinal model is shown to be particularly useful for biological populations. Estimation and prediction is demonstrated using integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA) methods developed for univariate spatio-temporal models. Bayesian estimation and prediction shows that the four invasive weed species differentially respond to habitat type, control effort and accessibility, and share similar magnitudes of dependence with short effective spatial ranges and strong temporal autocorrelations.

items.title: Multi-scale analysis of the agricultural phosphorus cycle in Norway to inform farm, regional, and national resource efficiency strategies
items.abstract: Abstract Ineffective phosphorus (P) management in agriculture raises concerns about resource depletion, supply security, eutrophication, and biodiversity loss. A major barrier to more circular and resource-efficient P management is the spatial imbalance between farms: livestock farms often accumulate surplus P from manure in soil, whereas crop farms typically face P deficits that are met with mineral fertilizers. Yet models capable of testing strategies to address these spatial inefficiencies remain limited. We study how a multi‑scale analysis can guide strategies to reduce P imports and soil accumulation in Norway. Using Substance Flow Analysis and farm subsidy statistics, we quantify the P cycles of ~40 000 farms (2019–2023) and aggregate results to municipal, county, and national levels. We then test four manure‑redistribution strategies: on‑farm optimization, and trade at the municipal, county, and national levels. We find that Norwegian agriculture applies 22,1 kt P·yr⁻ 1 to cropland; 4% is lost to runoff and 41% accumulates in soils, particularly in the livestock‑dense Western regions. 9% of harvested crop P is used for direct human consumption, compared to 91% for animal feed. On‑farm optimization reduces mineral P use by 38% and soil accumulation by 36%; municipal and national trade of manure lower P imports by 61% and 78%, and soil accumulation by 65% and 80%, respectively. We provide a reproducible method to build national multi-scale P analyses. Results help identify spatial barriers to circular strategies, indicating where local management is sufficient and where further processing and trade are required.

items.title: Context-dependent dispersal directionality in a headwater stream salamander
items.abstract: Abstract Background Dispersal is an integral component of population dynamics that comes with both fitness costs and benefits. Behavioral adaptations that minimize dispersal costs, such as non-random directionality, occur across taxa. However, most studies on directionality focus on single-risk (or single-benefit) systems even though organisms are likely subject to multiple co-occurring risk factors that may influence directionality in different ways. Methods Here, we used 12y of spatially explicit capture-mark-recapture data to investigate variation in dispersal directionality based on the spatial location of individual salamanders ( Gyrinophilus porphyriticus : N = 1375). Each summer, we conducted weekly surveys across 1000 m of three independent headwater streams to quantify movement dynamics based on life history stage. Results We found that adult, but not larval, salamanders are more likely to disperse upstream in downstream reaches, and more likely to disperse downstream in upstream reaches, consistent with our initial expectations given the risk landscape present in these systems. Specifically, we found that adult salamanders in the furthest upstream portions of the stream are approximately 1.74 times more likely to disperse downstream than those at the base of the stream, which were more likely to disperse upstream. Conclusions Regardless of direction, the proportion of salamanders that dispersed was consistent across three populations, suggesting that dispersal propensity is unrelated to dispersal directionality. Our results suggest that context-dependent directionality may represent a common source of individual-level variation in dispersal behavior for this species. Assessments of context-dependent directionality in other species may improve models of animal movement.

items.title: Host-Specific Gut Microbiota in Sympatric Honey Bees: Contrasting Microbial Diversity Between Native Melipona scutellaris and Managed Apis mellifera in the Atlantic Forest
items.abstract: Abstract Bees are essential pollinators with diverse gut microbiomes that vary across species and environments. While the microbiota of managed Apis mellifera is well studied, knowledge about native tropical bees such as Melipona scutellaris remains limited. Understanding these microbial communities is crucial for pollinator conservation and management. We characterized and compared the intestinal microbiota of worker bees from A. mellifera and M. scutellaris collected in the Atlantic forest biome. Composite samples of workers from each species were analyzed using high-throughput sequencing of bacterial marker genes, followed by standardized bioinformatic and statistical approaches to assess taxonomic composition, diversity, and community structure. Results revealed distinct, species-specific gut microbiota profiles. M. scutellaris harbored a larger number of core bacterial taxa and exhibited greater phylogenetic diversity, whereas A. mellifera showed a more restricted but dominant core community. Only five taxa were shared between species. Phylogenetic diversity was significantly higher in M. scutellaris (Faith index: 12.736 vs 7.412, p = 0.009), while Shannon and Pielou indices showed no significant differences. Beta diversity analyses indicated structural differences between species (PERMANOVA: Jaccard p = 0.006; Bray-Curtis p = 0.003; UniFrac weighted p = 0.011; UniFrac unweighted p = 0.008). ANCOM identified Lactobacillus , Anthococcus , and Bifidobacterium as the most differentially abundant taxa, with Anthococcus absent in A. mellifera . Therefore, despite sharing the same environment, the two bee species maintain structurally distinct gut microbiotas, reflecting host specificity and evolutionary adaptation. These findings provide baseline information on native stingless bee microbiomes and contribute to strategies for conserving and managing tropical pollinators.

items.title: The role of tree cover in enhancing paddock resilience: insights from remote sensing in amazonian silvopastoral systems
items.abstract: Abstract Silvopastoral systems are vital for enhancing tropical pasture sustainability and mitigating degradation, yet their temporal dynamics under varying climates remain insufficiently quantified. This study evaluated the influence of tree cover on vegetation dynamics in an Amazonian silvopastoral system from 2016 to 2025. Sentinel-2 derived Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Normalized Difference Moisture Index (NDMI) time series were analyzed across 110 paddocks, utilizing Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS to assess long-term trends and seasonal patterns. Tree cover percentage, extracted from Unmanned Aerial Vehicle imagery, was used to stratify paddocks. Results demonstrated that higher tree cover consistently correlated with elevated NDVI and NDMI values. During periods of lower precipitation (2019–2022), paddocks with greater tree cover exhibited slower declines and faster recoveries, indicating enhanced resistance to hydrological stress and reduced intra-annual variability. Statistical modeling revealed a significant negative association between tree cover and NDVI amplitude during specific drier years (2019, 2020, and 2022), indicating greater seasonal spectral stability alongside an overall increase in dry-season NDVI. However, during the extreme 2024 drier condition, differences among classes diminished, suggesting limits to the trees’ buffering capacity. These findings indicate that higher tree cover was associated with greater stability and resilience in the studied pasture system under moderate climatic stress, though extreme conditions can constrain these effects. Ultimately, this study highlights scattered trees as a key structural component, suggesting their potential role in strategies to bolster silvopasture resilience across the Amazonian agricultural frontier.

items.title: Studying Chars in South Asia: Towards an Epistemic Approach
items.abstract: The epistemologies based on the terra firma framework fall short in interpreting the relationship and transcendence of land and water concerning the river islands ( chars ). Consequently, the ways of life associated with these inhabited islands are also not considered along with the fluidities of its geography. This article examines the chars of two major river systems in two regional states of India (the Ganga in West Bengal and the Brahmaputra in Assam) through a ‘geo-morpho-anthropology’ approach that brings together the geographical, morphological, and anthropological dimensions of chars in order to understand the embedded flux associated in the relationship between land and water. It studies the continual changes caused by river erosion and accretion, and how people dwelling on these islands sustain their lives. Through an integrated perspective, we seek to present an epistemic approach to study chars in large river systems in South Asia.

items.title: EUBURN: The southern Europe biomass burning programme
items.abstract: Southern Europe is experiencing a shift towards a new wildfire regime, characterised by larger and more intense fires, and an extension of the fire season beyond the traditional summer months. Climate projections indicate that the occurrence and severity of fwildfires will increase faster than the global average due to an increased risk of heatwaves and droughts. These conditions are expected to reduce fuel moisture, extend the fire season and increase the likelihood of large and severe wildfires. At the same time, changes in fire regimes may alter vegetation composition and ecosystem structure, potentially favouring fire-adapted species while threatening species that are less resilient to increasingly frequent or severe fires. Addressing these emerging challenges require new tools and technologies needed to implement comprehensive fire management approaches. The community still faces challenges in predicting which wildfires may escalate into extreme events, and the environmental, climate and health impacts of the associated smoke remain poorly understood. The southern Europe biomass BURNing (EUBURN) programme was developed in response to the need to improve the prevention, monitoring and prediction of wildfire risks in southern Europe. EUBURN integrates multi-year, multi-scale field campaigns, laboratory studies, satellite remote sensing and advanced modelling to establish the research foundations for understanding the complex interactions between wildfires and the atmosphere. Based on this fundamental research, the programme aims to support fire responders, ecosystems and air quality management, while addressing specific climate research requirements by developing new or enhanced operational products, tools and services for predicting and monitoring wildfires and their associated smoke plumes. This article provides an overview of EUBURN, including its motivation and design. It also describes the measurements and modelling strategy that will be employed to fulfil the programme's scientific objectives.

items.title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of the Hong Kong Krabby Harvestman (Heterobiantes geniculatus) (Opiliones: Epedanidae)
items.abstract: Abstract Harvestmen (order Opiliones) are a diverse order within Arachnida that are widely distributed across the globe, and are known for their ecological roles as detritivores and predators in terrestrial ecosystems. However, the scarcity of high-quality genomic resources, especially for Asian endemic lineages, has hindered research into their morphological adaptations and evolutionary history. Here, we generated a chromosome-level genome assembly for the Hong Kong Krabby Harvestman ( Heterobiantes geniculatus ), a species endemic to Asia belonging to the family Epedanidae (Opiliones: Laniatores), by integrating PacBio HiFi long reads, Illumina short reads, RNA-seq, and Hi-C chromatin conformation capture technologies. The final genome assembly spans 3.15 Gb, with a scaffold N50 of 101.15 Mb, and a contig N50 of 8.10 Mb. Notably, 82.91% of the assembly was anchored onto 25 pseudochromosomes, and BUSCO assessment revealed a high genome completeness of 97.4%, indicating excellent assembly quality. This chromosome-level genome represents the first high-quality genomic resource for the genus Heterobiantes , providing a critical foundation for future investigations into the genetic basis of its specialized phenotypic adaptations, reconstructing the evolutionary history of Epedanidae, and resolving phylogenetic controversies within Opiliones.

items.title: A systematic review of Islamic green finance: Trends, challenges, and future directions
items.abstract: Purpose – This study systematically reviews Islamic green finance (IGF) literature to chart its scholarly evolution, identify key thematic research streams, and propose a structured future research agenda. Design – This systematic review combines bibliometric analysis (co-citation, co-authorship, and keyword co-occurrence mapping) with qualitative content analysis of 317 Scopus-indexed documents (journal articles and book chapters) published between 2010 and 2025, and selected following PRISMA 2020. Findings – Research output is concentrated in Malaysia and Indonesia, and more than four-fifths of the documents were published from 2021 onward. Five research streams are identified: (1) global practices and frameworks; (2) ethics, ESG and fintech governance; (3) innovative instruments for the SDGs; (4) institutional risk and sustainability; and (5) hybrid instruments. Green sukuk still dominate, while impact measurement remains the least developed area. The study proposes 31 future research questions linked to the gaps in each stream. Research Implications – The review relies on a single database (Scopus) and English-language documents, combines journal articles with book chapters and does not include a formal quality appraisal. Citation-based clustering may also under-represent recent work. Originality – Earlier reviews concentrate on a single instrument, such as green or SRI sukuk, or on a single country. This review maps the wider IGF field across 317 documents from 139 sources and links five research streams to a structured agenda of 31 questions.

items.title: AVALIAÇÃO ESPACIAL E TEMPORAL DA QUALIDADE DA ÁGUA DO RIO URAIM SOB DIFERENTES PRESSÕES ANTRÓPICAS EM PARAGOMINAS, PARÁ
items.abstract: As transformações no uso e ocupação da terra podem comprometer a qualidade das águas superficiais, especialmente em bacias hidrográficas submetidas à expansão urbana e agropecuária. Este estudo objetivou avaliar as variações espaciais e temporais da qualidade da água do Rio Uraim, em Paragominas, Pará, considerando possíveis associações com pressões antrópicas. A pesquisa apresentou caráter descritivo e exploratório, com abordagem predominantemente quantitativa, abrangendo dez pontos de amostragem distribuídos ao longo do trecho investigado, em campanhas realizadas em janeiro e abril. Foram analisados parâmetros físicos, químicos e microbiológicos, interpretados individualmente e de forma integrada, utilizando como referência comparativa os padrões da Resolução CONAMA nº 357/2005 para águas doces de Classe 2. Os resultados evidenciaram aumento da demanda bioquímica de oxigênio (DBO) e redução da turbidez em todos os pontos na campanha de abril, além de variações nas concentrações de nutrientes e coliformes termotolerantes, com alterações mais expressivas entre P6 e P10. Embora os valores de DBO e oxigênio dissolvido tenham atendido aos limites de referência considerados, foram identificados valores de pH inferiores à faixa estabelecida, concentrações elevadas de fósforo total e coliformes termotolerantes em determinados pontos e turbidez superior a 100 UNT em parte das amostras. Essas diferenças sugerem possíveis associações com as condições naturais da bacia e as pressões decorrentes das atividades humanas, sem permitir estabelecer relações causais diretas. A ausência de valores finais do Índice de Qualidade da Água (IQA) e de dados hidrológicos simultâneos limitou a avaliação quantitativa integrada e a interpretação da influência sazonal. Conclui-se que o Rio Uraim apresenta heterogeneidade espacial e temporal nos indicadores de qualidade da água, evidenciando a necessidade de monitoramento contínuo e de estratégias integradas de conservação e gestão dos recursos hídricos.

items.title: The Vāhana Tradition and the Ecological Wisdom of Sanātana Dharma
items.abstract: The Vāhana Tradition and the Ecological Wisdom of Sanātana Dharma Divinity, Biodiversity and the Interconnectedness of Life Yogesh Arvind Puranik Chairman, AnuYog Sansthan ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0005-7073-9737 Book DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24224023 ABSTRACT This study investigates the vāhana tradition, the divine vehicles and animal associations of Hindu deities, as a central and distinctive point of connection between Sanātana Dharma and contemporary ecological thought. It asks how animals made visible in divine narratives, images, temple settings, processions and worship may acquire cultural significance, and whether that significance can shape human attitudes towards the living beings they represent. The vāhana is examined not merely as an iconographic attribute, but as a religious and cultural relationship through which non-human life becomes present within the sacred world of communities. Across twenty-four chapters, the book traces the historical development and varied forms of vāhana associations, then studies individual cases including Nandi, Garuḍa, the lion and tiger of Durgā, the peacock of Kārttikeya, Gaṇeśa’s mouse, the haṃsa, Airāvata, the owl, makara, buffalo, antelope and dog. It also considers regional traditions and related sacred-animal relationships, while distinguishing formal vāhanas from companions, narrative animals, divine manifestations and local ritual associations. Each case is approached through textual, historical, iconographic and, where relevant, zoological and ecological evidence. The study asks what biological animal is represented, what ecological role that animal performs, what religious meanings attach to it, and whether evidence supports any connection between reverence, restraint, care or conservation. The vāhana inquiry is situated within a wider examination of Sanātana Dharma’s ecological resources: ṛta and interconnectedness, the Bhūmi Sūkta’s vision of Earth, ahiṃsā and dharma, sacred trees, rivers, forests and landscapes, and documented community practices. It then brings these materials into dialogue with modern ecology and biodiversity conservation. The book’s central contribution is its sustained, case-by-case interpretation of the vāhana tradition as a possible cultural bridge between religious symbolism and ecological responsibility. It does not claim that ancient communities possessed modern ecological science, that every vāhana association protected its species, or that symbolic reverence proves conservation outcomes. Rather, it distinguishes religious meaning, cultural transmission, observed conduct and measurable ecological effects. It argues that vāhana traditions offer a significant and under-examined resource for contemporary reflection on biodiversity, while identifying where historical and empirical evidence supports, qualifies or limits that claim.

items.title: Consumers’ knowledge of the environmental footprint of food categories: evidence from a controlled experiment without and after label exposure
items.abstract: Purpose The study aims to investigate whether consumers are able to correctly assess the environmental footprint of food categories and whether exposure to environmental labels during a shopping task improves their knowledge. Design/methodology/approach A total of 577 non-student participants completed a knowledge test after being exposed, during a shopping task, to one of six environmental labelling formats or no label at all. The test assessed three dimensions: the ability to rank food categories by environmental impact (ordinal ranking), estimate the magnitude of impact differences between categories (cardinal ranking) and perceive within-category footprint variability. Responses from labelled and unlabelled groups were compared to evaluate both overall and format-specific impacts on knowledge. Findings Participants were relatively accurate in identifying the most and least impactful food categories but significantly underestimated the scale of differences between them – especially the gap between red meat and other food groups. Within-category variability was generally overestimated. Exposure to environmental labels only slightly improved knowledge, with modest gains observed for the fish and fruits, vegetables and pulses categories. One label format, which benchmarked impact within food categories, actually worsened knowledge by reinforcing existing misconceptions. Research limitations/implications Findings are limited to immediate effects from a single shopping task. Long-term exposure to labels may yield different results. Moreover, the knowledge test design (using a 0–100 slider) may be subject to framing effects. Practical implications Consumers underestimate the environmental benefits of switching between food categories – particularly from animal-based categories (and especially red meat) to plant-based categories – and overestimate those within categories. Policymakers should help consumers identify the most impactful dietary changes. Caution is warranted when using category-based benchmarking, as it may mislead consumers and promote less effective dietary shifts. Social implications This study highlights the importance of improving consumer knowledge about the environmental impact of food choices. By identifying gaps and misperceptions in how individuals compare broad food categories, the findings support the development of environmental labels that can guide more sustainable dietary decisions. Enhancing public understanding at this level is essential for fostering collective behavioural shifts towards lower-impact diets, contributing to climate and environmental goals through informed consumer action. Originality/value This study introduces a novel method to measure consumer environmental knowledge and is among the first to evaluate the effect of short-term exposure to environmental labels on such knowledge. It distinguishes between types of knowledge – ordinal, cardinal and variability-related – providing a nuanced understanding of consumers’ misperception regarding the environmental footprint of food.

items.title: Complex lake effects structure bryophyte communities across spatial scales around Lake Superior, Canada.
items.abstract: Context Studies have found that large lakes significantly modify regional climates, an influence known as the "lake effect". Large lakes may provide biodiversity refugia in a changing climate owing to the lake effect, but the impacts of lake effects on biodiversity remain poorly documented. Objectives We sought to quantify the influence of the lake effect on bryophyte communities in the vicinity of Lake Superior, and to disentangle the lake effect from processes occurring at larger (regional) and smaller (forest stand) scales. Methods We sampled bryophyte communities on three substrates (trees, rocks, and logs) across 54 sites on and near the northern and eastern shores of Lake Superior. We combined community data with climate and forest data to determine the influence of variables at each of three spatial scales-micro (forest attributes), meso (lake effect), and macro (regional climatic norms)-on community composition and richness. Results The lake effect structured community composition, along with regional climate norms and forest characteristics. The lake effect was divided into three orthogonal axes. Notably, each of these axes included a distinct component of the moisture environment-precipitation, relative humidity, and vapour pressure deficit-and our results suggest that these components have divergent effects on bryophyte communities. The lake effect had no significant influence on species richness. Conclusions Lake Superior induces biotically important climatic heterogeneity that structures bryophyte communities across the study region. The near-lake environment may be an important thermal and hydrologic refuge for bryophytes in a warming, drying climate. Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10980-026-02488-8.

items.title: On R-Matrix Formulation of qq-Characters
items.abstract: Abstract We introduce an R -matrix formulation of qq -characters and corresponding Frenkel–Reshetikhin deformed W -algebras. The R -matrix featuring in the construction is of Ding–Iohara–Miki (DIM) algebra, while the type of the qq -character is determined by the network of Fock representations corresponding to a web of 5-branes geometrically engineering a quiver gauge theory.Our formulation gives a unified description of qq -characters of $$A_n$$ A n type and their elliptic uplifts.

items.title: Benchmarking AI-evolved cosmological structure formation
items.abstract: Abstract The potential of deep learning-based image-to-image translations has attracted significant attention as a fast, approximate alternative to cosmological simulations, which would be particularly useful in various contexts, including covariance studies, investigations of systematics, and cosmological parameter inference. We model the evolution of structure formation using U-Net, a widely employed convolutional image translation framework with previous applications in cosmology. To study aspects of learning-based cosmological mappings in a controlled, illustrative setting, we use two approaches for generating suitable cosmological matter fields as datasets: a simple analytical prescription provided by the Zel’dovich approximation, and a standard N-body method using Particle-Mesh simulations. We apply established metrics such as matter power spectra and bispectra, topological indicators, and statistical independence of density fields and study their reproducibility and convergence properties. The U-Net approach performs well only for some of these physical metrics, and accuracy is worse at more nonlinear scales, where the dynamic range in density is larger. Motivated by field-level emulator studies utilizing Eulerian-aware loss functions and beyond pixel-wise mean squared errors, we examine a density-weighted objective. In the PM tests ending at z = 4, where the evolution is only mildly nonlinear, using the Eulerian matter density evaluated at each particle position as a direct weight on that particle’s Lagrangian displacement error improves the U-Net results at smaller scales; this result does not establish comparable accuracy in the strongly nonlinear low-redshift regime.

items.title: Functional and Density-Driven Errors in Density Functional Theory: Quantum Monte Carlo Benchmarks for Solids
items.abstract: Abstract We introduce a systematic analysis of density functional approximation errors in solids by separating functional-driven from density-driven contributions using quantum Monte Carlo densities of silicon, sodium chloride, and copper as reference. Typically, functional errors dominate, but we identify important exceptions where the xc component of the density-driven error exceeds the functional error, notably for SOGGA11 in the semiconductor and the insulator. Material dependence is striking: 61% of functionals show error cancellation in silicon versus 16% in copper, and only five functionals surpass LDA accuracy for metallic copper even with exact densities. For silicon and sodium chloride, GILL or BECKE exchange combined with PBE, PW91, or P86 correlation achieves near-exact xc energies on QMC densities, while copper requires specialized functionals like PBEsol or PBELYP. High-quality densities consistently reduce density-driven errors across all systems. Historical analysis reveals that 1990s GGA functionals outperform many modern meta-GGAs, contradicting expectations of systematic improvement along Jacob’s ladder. These results provide practical guidance for functional selection and highlight implications for machine learning potential development, where material-dependent error cancellation may compromise transferability.

items.title: From London to Morse via Binnig, Quate, and Gerber
items.abstract: Summary In their landmark paper introducing the atomic force microscope [Phys. Rev. Lett. 56 , 930 (1986)], Binnig, Quate, and Gerber presciently anticipated that the technique would ultimately be capable of probing interactions running the gamut from weak van der Waals interactions to strong covalent bonding. They also highlighted that the tip‐sample forces central to AFM are present, and often highly influential, in scanning tunnelling microscopy; indeed, this realisation directly inspired the invention of the force microscope. In this perspective for the Forty Years of AFM special issue, we review selected aspects of two decades of work from our group at the University of Nottingham that span the force range highlighted by BQG and are united by a common, central theme: the probe as active participant rather than passive observer. Our selection of results also covers length and correlation scales from the microscopic right down to the single chemical bond limit, tracking a spectrum of interactions from van der Waals/Hamaker forces, through hydrogen bonding, to covalent bonds and, finally, atom‐by‐atom assembly of metal clusters via vertical tip‐sample transfer. Echoing BQG's own observations on the prevalence of probe‐sample forces in STM, we also discuss recent evidence that tip‐induced heterogeneity underpins first‐passage dynamics in molecular diffusion and highlight the challenges in acquiring non‐invasive measurements of diffusion barriers for adsorbed molecules that are readily perturbed by the probe. We close with a perspective on machine learning's growing role in automating tip‐driven atomic and molecular manipulation.

items.title: Low-Redshift Analogues of the First Galaxies
items.abstract: This study investigates whether low-metallicity galaxies in the nearby Universe can act as local analogues of high-redshift star-forming galaxies using spatially resolved spectroscopy from the SDSS-IV MaNGA survey. A cleaned sample of 9521 galaxies was constructed by combining MaNGA DRPall data with FIRE-FLY stellar population measurements. Galaxies were divided into three stellar mass bins, and low-metallicity analogue candidates were selected from the low-metallicity tails of the stellar mass–metallicity relation using mass-dependent metallicity thresholds of Z < −0.5, Z < −0.4 and Z < −0.25. This produced final analogue samples of 46 low-mass, 13 intermediate-mass and 13 high-mass galaxies. Matched comparison galaxies wereselected using stellar mass and (u − r) color constraints. Spatially resolved MaNGA maps were analyzed to investigate stellar and ionized gas kinematics. Stellar velocity dispersions of low and intermediate-mass analogue galaxies were broadly consistent with their matched counterparts, with median values of 52.8 km s−1 and 61.7 km s−1 respectively. However, high-mass analogue galaxies exhibited elevated stellar dispersions reaching a median of 201.2 km s−1, compared to 170.7 km s−1 in the control sample. Specific angular momentum measurements showed that the analogue population is overwhelmingly dominated by fast rotators. All low and intermediate-mass galaxies were classified as fast rotators, while 91.7% of the high-mass sample remained rotationally-supported. Median λR values were high across the sample, although high-mass analogue galaxies exhibited systematically lower angular momentum than their matched counterparts. The strongest differenceswere observed in the gas kinematics. High-mass analogue galaxies displayed extreme ionized gas velocity dispersions, with median Hα dispersions of 270.5 km s−1 compared to 107.4 km s−1 in the matched sample, indicating highly turbulent interstellar media. These results suggest that while most low-metallicity galaxies retain dynamically settled stellar disks, a subset of massive systems may reproduce the turbulent gas conditions characteristic of galaxies during the peak epoch of cosmic star formation. This work identifies galaxies that may resemble the physical conditions of star-forming systems at redshifts z ∼ 2 − 3, offering potential local analogues for studying galaxy evolution at cosmic noon.

items.title: A One-Way Energy Transfer Model Between Dark Matter and Dark Energy: A Conceptual Note
items.abstract: A One-Way Energy Transfer Model Between Dark Matter and Dark Energy: A Conceptual Note Author: Advik, Grade 9, Delhi, India Abstract Current cosmological models often assume dark matter and dark energy evolve independently, or exchange energy in both directions. This note proposes a simple conceptual alternative: a one-way transfer where energy flows from dark matter to dark energy, but not in reverse. We discuss why this idea is motivated by the observed decline of dark matter density and the dominance of dark energy at late times. We do not claim a full mathematical proof. The goal of this note is to present the idea clearly so it can be tested with DESI and future survey data in later work. 1. Introduction In the standard model, dark matter and dark energy are treated as separate components. Dark matter drives the formation of galaxies. Dark energy drives the accelerated expansion of the universe. As the universe expands, the universe changes from being matter-dominated to dark-energy-dominated. This note asks a simple question: What if these two changes are linked by a one-way transfer? 2. The Idea We propose that a small, continuous amount of energy leaks from the dark matter sector into the dark energy sector. The transfer is one-way only. Energy does not flow back from dark energy to dark matter. 3. Why One-Way? A two-way exchange would require a fine-tuned balance to avoid oscillations between the two components. A one-way flow is simpler and matches the arrow of time in cosmology: the universe goes from matter-dominated to dark-energy-dominated, and never goes back. 4. What Would Prove or Disprove It? This model is falsifiable. If future DESI data shows dark matter density falling faster than expected from expansion alone, while dark energy density rises by a matching amount, this model gains support. If the data shows no such matching change, the model is wrong. 5. Next Work The next step is to build a simple mathematical model with a coupling term and compare it to DESI BAO data. That will be the focus of Paper 2. Conclusion This note does not solve dark energy. It proposes a simpler way to think about the relationship between dark matter and dark energy. If the idea is wrong, it can be tested and rejected quickly. If it is right, it gives a new direction for future work. References 1. DESI Collaboration, Adame, A. G. et al. items.title: Loneliness and the social brain: the mediating role of social functioning between nucleus accumbens structure and loneliness in aging.
items.abstract: Loneliness is a complex and distressing emotional state linked to impaired health and well-being in later life. Although its behavioral and social correlates are well documented, the neural mechanisms underlying loneliness remain less clear. The nucleus accumbens (NAcc) plays a central role in reward processing and social motivation, suggesting its potential involvement in loneliness. The present study examined whether individual differences in loneliness are associated with structural variation in the NAcc, and whether social functioning mediates this relationship. Using high-resolution structural MRI in a sample of elderly participants, we measured NAcc volume and assessed loneliness alongside validated indices of social functioning. Results indicated that smaller NAcc volume was significantly related to higher loneliness, and this association was statistically consistent with an indirect effect via reduced social functioning. These findings highlight the neural underpinnings of loneliness in aging and underscore the importance of social functioning as a pathway linking brain structure to subjective social experience.

items.title: Accuracy of different methods for predicting proximity to failure during resistance training.
items.abstract: Proximity to failure (PTF) is increasingly considered in resistance training (RT). Two common methods used to prescribe PTF are rating of perceived exertion (RPE) and repetitions in reserve (RIR). This study compared the accuracy of RIR and RPE for predicting PTF. In a randomised crossover design, 32 participants (19 trained, 13 untrained) completed machine chest press and leg extension exercises at 75% of one-repetition maximum. Participants completed two experimental sessions, one using RIR and one using Borg-RPE. Experimental session (RIR/RPE) and exercise order were randomised. During each set, participants indicated when they believed they had reached 2 RIR or 8 RPE and then continued to momentary failure. Accuracy was calculated as the difference between actual repetitions remaining to failure and the number predicted at the verbal call. No significant differences in accuracy were observed between RIR and Borg-RPE for either exercise (chest press: mean difference -0.03 repetitions, 95% CI - 0.50 to 0.44, p = 0.893; leg extension: mean difference 0.16 repetitions, 95% CI - 0.39 to 0.71, p = 0.556). Training status did not influence the difference in accuracy between methods. These findings indicate that Borg-RPE and RIR produce similar accuracy when estimating PTF during machine-based RT under the conditions tested.

items.title: Neurophysiological evidence for rapid semantic integration via fast mapping.
items.abstract: Theories of declarative memory consolidation hold that novel associative information is integrated into cortical semantic networks slowly and with hippocampal support. However, an encoding paradigm called fast mapping (FM) has been proposed to permit rapid cortical integration of novel item-label associations, particularly when the novel item shares substantial visual-semantic features with a simultaneously presented known concept. We tested whether associations encoded through FM immediately engage semantic memory networks, indexed by the N400 event-related potential. In contrast to behavioral semantic priming tasks, in which semantic relatedness and response congruency may be confounded, the present EEG study provides a more process-specific test of rapid semantic integration. Sixty participants encoded pairs of a novel item and an unfamiliar label under two conditions, differing with respect to the visual-semantic overlap between the novel item and a simultaneously presented known item. In a subsequent semantic priming task, the novel labels served as primes for semantically related versus unrelated targets. While behavioral results did not reveal a significant priming effect, EEG data indicated an N400 priming effect in the high-overlap FM condition, characterized by reduced N400 amplitudes for related compared with unrelated targets over a parietal electrode cluster. Crucially, the N400 effect was significantly larger after high-overlap FM than after low-overlap FM encoding, indicating that high feature overlap enhances rapid semantic integration already minutes after learning. These findings provide the first neurophysiological evidence that high-overlap FM enables rapid semantic integration.

items.title: Benchmarking genome-wide association study causal gene prioritization for drug discovery.
items.abstract: Drug discovery is costly, with billions spent on failed trials. Drugs with genetic support from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have substantially greater odds of success, but how best to use GWAS to prioritize drug targets remains unclear. We evaluated the performance of GWAS causal gene prioritization methods from the Open Targets consortium by cross-referencing their predictions with drug trial outcomes for 445 diseases. We found that neither expression quantitative trait locus colocalization nor Open Targets' locus-to-gene (L2G) score outperformed the simple nearest-gene method at prioritizing which genes would become approved drug targets. Our findings inform the use of genetic evidence in drug discovery.

items.title: Exploring the pathogenesis underlying development of bronchopulmonary dysplasia in preterm infants using serum multi-proteomics.
items.abstract: The increasing incidence and lack of effective strategies for the prevention of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) in preterm infants underlines the need to gain further insight into molecular changes associated with the development of this condition. To quantify serum protein levels in preterm infants (<30 weeks gestational age (GA)) associated with molecular mechanisms underlying BPD development. Serum samples, collected at birth, day 3, 7, and 14, of 64 preterm infants (of whom 18 were diagnosed with BPD) were analyzed using proteomic approaches. Cross-sectional statistical analysis revealed the levels of 80 out of 665 quantified proteins differed between the infants with and without BPD, with most alterations found on day 3 (n = 59) and day 7 (n = 40). Notably, the majority of proteins were decreased in infants developing BPD. Alterations included growth factors (e.g., insulin like growth factor (IGF) pathway components), immunoglobulins, and circulating blood cell-derived proteins, alongside a clear cytokine disruption. The affected pathways underscore the broad dysregulation of processes besides inflammation in preterm infants who developed BPD. These findings may provide a basis for studies searching for alternative therapeutic targets to prevent BPD. The incidence of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) in preterm infants is increasing. Multi-proteomic analysis of longitudinal serum samples in the first two weeks after birth can identify molecular changes associated with BPD development. The majority of proteins levels were decreased in preterm infants who developed BPD with most pronounced differences at day 3 and day 7 Alterations were observed in levels of cytokines, insulin-like growth factor related proteins, immunoglobulins as well as circulating blood-cell-derived protein signatures. This study highlights molecular alterations beyond inflammation and suggests a broader change in molecular processes related to systemic communication.

items.title: Predictive performance of lifestyle-informed multimodal brain features for cognition in healthy older adults.
items.abstract: Identifying neuroimaging markers of cognitive performance in healthy aging is challenging due to heterogeneity in brain and cognitive characteristics. Among the factors relevant to that heterogeneity are lifestyle choices, of which each individual factor explains only a very small amount of variance in brain and cognition. This challenges current approaches for the prediction of cognitive outcomes. We examined whether brain features associated with an overall lifestyle profile (BF-Life multi ) provide predictive information for 13 cognitive outcomes compared with those related to single lifestyle factors (BF-Life single ), in 774 participants from the 1000BRAINS study (age: 67.0 ± 6.7 years), cross-sectionally and longitudinally (4-year follow-up). The BF-Life multi model showed modest domain-specific prediction, with the highest performance for baseline figural memory, primarily involving regions within the salience/ventral attention, default mode, somatomotor, and visual networks. These models did not consistently outperform data-driven models based on general brain features with shared variance alone. Including demographic variables improved prediction, whereas individual lifestyle factors added little benefit. No model reliably predicted longitudinal cognitive outcomes. Overall, lifestyle-related brain differences can contribute domain-specific complementary information for cognitive performance prediction in aging, but are not generalizable across domains and for capturing intraindividual trajectories.

items.title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in adults with overweight/obesity and alcohol use disorder: A retrospective cohort study.
items.abstract: Background Emerging evidence suggests glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) may improve outcomes in alcohol use disorder (AUD), which is associated with cardiovascular risk and mortality. Objective Evaluate the association between initiation of GLP-1RAs and clinical outcomes among adults with AUD and overweight or obesity. Design A retrospective cohort study using electronic health records from TriNetX research network, with participants enrolled between January 1, 2015 and December 31, 2024 and followed through December 31, 2025. Inverse probability of treatment weighting, based on propensity scores, balanced baseline characteristics. Weighted logistic regression models estimated the adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) at 1-year follow-up. Participants Adults ≥18 years old with overweight or obesity and AUD, without prior GLP-1RAs, or cancer or non-nicotine substance use disorder diagnoses. Interventions At least one GLP-1RA prescription issued after enrollment (Treatment cohort); none for Controls. Measures Presence (Yes/No) of all-cause and alcohol-related hospitalizations, mortality, and major cardiovascular events (MCVE) since the GLP-1RA initiation (Treatment cohort) or post-enrollment (Control cohort). Results Among 163,681 participants (mean age 53.7 ± 14.4 years; 35.6% female), 10,445 (6.4%) initiated GLP-1RAs. At 1-year follow-up, Treatment cohort had lower likelihood of all-cause (aOR=0.28, 95%CI: 0.28,0.29) and alcohol-related (aOR=0.20; 95%CI: 0.20,0.21) hospitalizations, death (aOR=0.20, 95%CI: 0.19,0.21), and MCVE (aOR=0.72, 95%CI: 0.71,0.74). Exploratory analyses showed that these associations remained consistent at 3 and 5 years. Conclusion GLP-1RA initiation was associated with reduced risk of MCVE, hospitalization, and mortality among adults with AUD and overweight/obesity, supporting potential role of GLP-RAs in AUD. Prospective studies are warranted.

items.title: A hypothesis framework linking the menopausal transition, sleep and brain waste clearance: Insights from experimental models.
items.abstract: The menopausal transition is increasingly recognized as a neuroendocrine transition with implications for brain health, sleep, cognition and vulnerability to neurodegenerative disease. Fluctuating and declining ovarian hormones coincide with sleep disruption, vasomotor symptoms, cognitive complaints, neuroinflammation and altered blood-brain barrier integrity. Current preclinical models each capture selected components of the menopause transition and provide essential mechanistic insights into the effect of ovarian hormone loss on the brain. Across these models, endocrine change is associated with impairments in hippocampal and prefrontal-dependent cognition, altered sleep-wake regulation, vascular dysfunction, glial activation, disrupted synaptic and mitochondrial homeostasis and exacerbation of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease-like pathology. An emerging but understudied mechanism linking menopause, sleep and neurodegeneration is the glymphatic system, a sleep-dependent brain waste clearance pathway. This review synthesises current evidence to highlight how menopause-related sleep disruption, vascular dysfunction, neuroinflammation and potential alterations in brain-waste clearance may converge to shape cognitive ageing and neurodegenerative disease risk.

items.title: Acoustic stimuli-enhanced environmental enrichment remodulates cortical processing of sound azimuth in adult female rats.
items.abstract: Acoustic stimuli-enhanced environmental enrichment (AEE) has been shown to significantly facilitate the behavioral and neuronal processing of sound by promoting plasticity in the auditory system. However, the mechanisms through which acoustic stimulation contributes to enrichment-induced effects remain largely unexplored. Here we found that AEE exposure during adulthood significantly improved the sound-azimuth discrimination abilities of female rats compared to age-matched naïve controls. Furthermore, AEE enhanced the sound-azimuth selectivity of neurons in the primary auditory cortex. These changes in the behavioral and cortical processing of sound azimuth were accompanied by an increase in the density of cortical parvalbumin-labeled (PV+) inhibitory interneurons. Interestingly, the rats reared in an identical enriched condition but without extra sound exposure also exhibited sharper cortical azimuth tuning and more cortical PV+ interneurons compared to the naïve rats. However, the post-rearing effects in these rats were less pronounced than those observed in the AEE rats, indicating an additional contribution of acoustic stimulation to enrichment-induced changes in the mature auditory cortex. Together, these findings provide compelling evidence for the significant influence of AEE on behavioral and cortical processing of sound azimuth. They suggest that AEE is an effective paradigm for promoting experience-dependent plasticity in the auditory system, even beyond the traditionally recognized critical period.

items.title: Baseline suicidal thoughts are associated with ECT non-remission and cognitive side effects: A network outcome analysis.
items.abstract: Introduction Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is effective for severe depression, yet remission is not universal and cognitive side effects remain a concern. Individual depressive symptoms may provide prognostic information beyond overall severity scores. Methods In a multicentre cohort from the Dutch ECT Consortium, we applied network outcome analysis to seven symptoms harmonized across the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS). Outcomes were remission (N = 792) and in exploratory analysis, cognitive side effects (N = 100). Robustness was assessed through bootstrapping and sensitivity analyses, including established clinical predictors, an alternative remission definition, and multivariable logistic regression. Results Suicidal thoughts were associated with lower odds of remission (OR 0.77, bootstrapped confidence interval [bCI] 0.68-0.84) and higher odds of cognitive side effects (OR 1.34, bCI 1.15-2.02), with 98-100% and 72-91% bootstrap edge presence across sensitivity analyses, respectively. Reduced appetite was associated with higher remission odds (OR 1.08, bCI 1.03-1.22), with 70-94% bootstrap edge presence across sensitivity analyses, but the association was absent in the MADRS-specific analysis. Tension/anxiety was associated with higher odds of cognitive side effects (OR 1.26, bCI 1.14-1.92), with 77-84% bootstrap edge presence. After simultaneous covariate adjustment, logistic regression supported associations of suicidal thoughts with both outcomes and tension/anxiety with cognitive side effects; the adjusted cognitive model was exploratory. Conclusions Baseline symptoms showed distinct associations with ECT outcomes. Suicidal thoughts were associated with both lower remission likelihood and higher odds of cognitive side effects, suggesting potential relevance for clinical monitoring and counselling.

items.title: Choroid plexus volume as a marker of chronotherapeutic responsiveness in major depressive disorder.
items.abstract: Circadian rhythm disruption is a core feature of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). The choroid plexus (ChP), a circadian-regulated structure involved in cerebrospinal fluid production and immune signalling, has been previously associated with depression and may undergo structural changes in response to chronotherapeutics. The study included 25 patients with MDD and 25 matched healthy controls who underwent MRI. Patients received total sleep deprivation plus light therapy (TSD + LT), consisting of three 36-hour sleep deprivation cycles, each separated by a night of recovery sleep. LT was administered for 30 min every morning. Depressive symptoms, sleep quality, and chronotype were assessed through Beck's Depression Inventory (BDI), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ), respectively. ChP volumes were extracted with FreeSurfer and normalized for intracranial volume. Effects of chronotherapeutics were assessed on BDI, PSQI, and ChP volumes, with treatment response as a between-subject factor. The efficacy of treatment was also investigated stratifying for chronotype. Also, group differences in ChP volume and associations with sleep and BDI scores were explored. TSD + LT reduced depressive symptoms and improved sleep quality, with changes in PSQI associated with symptom improvement. Eveningness predicted greater depressive symptom reduction. At baseline, responders already exhibited larger left ChP volume than controls. Following treatment, a treatment × response interaction emerged for right ChP volume, showing a significant reduction in responders. Finally, reductions in both right and left ChP volumes predicted clinical improvement, and sleep quality improvement predicted right ChP volume reduction. This is the first study showing that chronotherapy modulates ChP structure in MDD, suggesting a link between circadian dysregulation and ChP enlargement proportional to clinical improvement and predicted by sleep amelioration. ChP volume may represent a biomarker of treatment responsiveness and circadian realignment.

items.title: Persistent neuroimmune alterations in children who are HIV-exposed but uninfected at age 6-7 years: Associations with language development in a South African birth cohort.
items.abstract: Children who are HIV-exposed but uninfected (HEU) are at increased risk of neurodevelopmental delays, yet neuroimmune pathways linking perinatal HIV exposure to school readiness remain unclear. In the Drakenstein Child Health Study, 267 children (93 HEU, 174 HIV-unexposed [HU]) underwent magnetic resonance spectroscopy in midline parietal grey and left parietal white matter regions at 6-7 years. Peripheral blood serum immune markers were measured in pregnancy and in children at 6 weeks, 2, 3, and 5 years. Linear mixed-effects models characterised child immune trajectories and linear regressions tested associations with creatine-referenced neurometabolite ratios and school readiness scores. Mothers living with HIV had higher sCD14 and lower MMP-9, NGAL, and GM-CSF than mothers without HIV (p < 0.05). Perinatal HIV exposure was associated with altered trajectories of child sCD14, GM-CSF, IL-1β, IL-5, IL-10, and YKL-40. At 6-7 years, children who were HEU had lower parietal grey matter glutamate ratios and lower left parietal white matter choline ratios. By school entry, more frequent associations between child immune markers and neurometabolites were observed, with IL-8 emerging as a recurrent correlate across developmental stages. Children who were HEU had lower language scores than HU peers. Left parietal white matter choline ratios were positively associated with language and overall school readiness in HU children, but not HEU. Perinatal HIV exposure was associated with alterations in immune development, neurometabolites reflecting both white matter maturation and neuronal health, and school readiness. Our findings highlight potential neuroimmune alterations contributing to neurodevelopmental risks in children who are HEU. A single explanatory pathway was not identified, supporting the need for longitudinal studies of neuroimmune, clinical, and environmental contributors to developmental vulnerability in this population.

items.title: EEG Microstate Alterations and Their Association with Cognitive Performance in Late-Onset Epilepsy of Unknown Etiology: Comparison with Alzheimer's Disease.
items.abstract: Background Cognitive impairment is common in late-onset epilepsy of unknown etiology (LOEU), but its electrophysiological correlates and relationship to Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain unclear. We compared resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) microstate dynamics among LOEU, AD, and cognitively normal (CN) groups and examined their associations with cognitive performance. Methods Eyes-closed 32-channel resting-state EEG recordings were analyzed from 60 patients with LOEU, 65 with AD, and 60 CN participants. Four canonical microstate classes (A-D) were identified. Group differences in microstate parameters were tested with false discovery rate correction. Associations with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores were examined using multivariable interaction models adjusted for age, sex, education, and cerebral small vessel disease burden. Results Microstate B duration was longer in LOEU and AD than in CN (Holm-adjusted p=0.011 and 0.016), whereas microstate C occurrence was lower in both patient groups (p=0.001 and 0.018). Microstate D duration was longer in LOEU than in CN and AD (both p=0.038). For microstate A duration, the group interaction survived false discovery rate correction for MMSE (q=0.0255) but not MoCA (q=0.122). In LOEU, longer microstate A duration was associated with lower MoCA and MMSE scores. Pairwise slope comparisons were more negative in LOEU than in CN for both outcomes, whereas LOEU-AD slope differences were not significant. Conclusions LOEU showed altered resting-state EEG microstate dynamics that partly overlapped with those observed in AD, alongside a group difference in microstate D duration. Microstate A duration was associated with cognitive performance in LOEU, although this association did not significantly differ from that observed in AD. These findings support further investigation of EEG microstates as electrophysiological correlates of cognitive dysfunction in LOEU while also highlighting overlap with AD.

items.title: Computer vision-aided locomotor behavioral analysis identifies therapeutic motor signatures in a mouse model of Huntington's disease.
items.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor dysfunction. Traditional open-field tests quantify spontaneous locomotor parameters but provide limited information on the duration and sequencing of individual movements across HD stages. Here, we applied a computer vision-aided behavioral flow analysis to quantify fine, HD-relevant motor dysfunction in the zQ175DN HD mouse model, from early to developed HD motor deficits. With DeepLabCut-tracked body movements, Keypoint-MoSeq identified recurrent behavioral syllables through unsupervised segmentation of standard top-view open-field recordings. These syllables were then grouped into behavioral clusters and analyzed for transitions between movements. Disease stage-dependent syllable occurrence and transition structure changes were identified. Genotype classification using syllable mean duration showed insufficient discrimination at 6 months and modest discrimination at 9 months, and combined behavioral features yielded higher discrimination at 12 months. HD was also associated with changes in which behavioral clusters served as hubs in the transition networks and the probabilities of switching between behaviors. We integrated these features into an HD motor dysfunction (HDMD) score based on deviations from age-matched wild-type (WT) reference values. The HDMD score distinguished zQ175DN mice from WT at multiple HD stages and aligned with HD pathology and disease severity. This HDMD scoring system may support retrospective analysis and more efficient preclinical drug-study design, as suggested by preliminary effect-size and power estimates assuming partial normalization of the HD phenotype. Overall, the HDMD score summarizes subtle motor abnormalities in HD mice and indicates further validation for preclinical drug efficacy assessment.

items.title: Spatial-Frequency-Dependent Temporal Dynamics of Orientation Ensemble Representation.
items.abstract: Average representation refers to the rapid extraction of the central tendency from a set of stimuli by the visual system. However, whether this efficient process relies on specific spatial frequency (SF) information remains poorly understood. To investigate the roles of low spatial frequency (LSF) and high spatial frequency (HSF) information in orientation ensemble averaging and the underlying temporal dynamics, we conducted two experiments combining behavioral and electroencephalographic (EEG) measures. Experiment 1 examined the effects of SF and visual field location on mean orientation judgments. Behavioral results indicated that LSF ensembles yielded superior accuracy and shorter reaction times compared to HSF ensembles, with performance further enhanced in the peripheral versus central visual field. To characterize the underlying temporal dynamics of ensemble processing, Experiment 2 focused on the peripheral field and utilized a neural adaptation paradigm in which the adapted and control test ensembles were matched in numerosity and spatial configuration. Electrophysiological results revealed a sequential processing trajectory: the LSF condition initially elicited a significant neural adaptation effect at the early C1 stage, followed by an HSF-elicited adaptation effect at the P1 stage. Finally, at the late P3 stage, the LSF condition exhibited a repetition enhancement effect. These findings suggest that orientation ensemble representation follows a spatial-frequency-dependent, coarse-fine-refine multistage dynamic pattern. Specifically, early LSF information facilitates a rapid, coarse holistic estimate; subsequently, HSF information contributes fine-grained details; and ultimately, the representation may be refined or calibrated through a late-stage process that may involve updating early LSF-based predictions.

items.title: Callosal atrophy does not establish physiological disconnection in imaging models of cognitive risk in multiple sclerosis.
items.abstract: Automated magnetic resonance imaging can quantify callosal atrophy and estimate structural disconnection in multiple sclerosis, but neither measurement establishes physiological conduction failure. In an early relapsing-remitting cohort, Wahl and colleagues found a relationship between motor-callosal microstructure and interhemispheric inhibition in controls that was not detectable in patients. This finding illustrates why a structural feature cannot automatically inherit a functional interpretation. Earlier structure-function studies provide a foundation for contemporary pipelines when the measurements, pathways, and populations are comparable. This opinion paper organizes validation into five evidence domains with separate biological and prognostic branches: technical validity, biological validity, physiological validity, prognostic performance, and clinical utility. Physiological claims require functional evidence matched to anatomy and task, with reliability and competing circuit explanations assessed. A purely prognostic feature instead requires credible predictive evaluation, including external validation and calibration; it may be useful as a proxy for global disease burden. Clinical utility concerns the consequences of a specified decision and is distinct from predictive performance and implementation feasibility. Reports should preserve the qualifier in estimated structural disconnection and reserve physiological interpretations for measurements supported by corresponding functional evidence.

items.title: Penetration depth, standalone coiling, and branch selection in middle meningeal artery embolization for chronic subdural hematoma: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Background Chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH) is increasingly treated with middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAe), but the impact of technical factors such as degree of penetration, standalone coiling, and the number of embolized branches remains poorly defined. We sought to perform a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine how these technical factors affect outcomes. Methods We performed a PRISMA‑guided systematic review and meta‑analysis of studies reporting on technical factors identified in PubMed, Scopus, Ovid Embase (Elsevier), and the Web of Science. Adults with nonacute subdural hematomas undergoing standalone or adjunct MMAe were included. Outcomes of interest included need for rescue treatment and radiographic success. Random effects models were used to obtain pooled estimates for each outcome. Results A total of 13 studies comprising 1,480 patients undergoing 1,727 embolizations were included. The weighted mean age was 70.8 years and 27.8% of patients were female. Onyx was the most common embolic agent used. Compared with distal penetration, proximal penetration was not significantly associated with radiographic success (OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.40-1.01; I 2 = 25.4%; P = 0.05) or rescue treatment (OR 1.60, 95% CI 0.67-3.81; I 2 = 0%; P = 0.29). Standalone coiling was not significantly associated with radiographic success (OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.77-2.21; I 2 = 0%) or rescue treatment (OR 1.20, 95% CI 0.43-3.38; I 2 = 0%; P = 0.73). There was also no significant difference in the odds of radiographic success (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.49-1.42; I 2 = 51.5%; P = 0.50) or rescue treatment (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.39-2.34; I 2 = 27.9%; P = 0.93) when comparing single versus multiple MMA branches embolized. Conclusions Degree of penetration, standalone coiling, and number of branches embolized were not significantly associated with outcomes in this limited meta-analysis. Although the point estimate favored distal penetration for radiographic success, the confidence interval included no difference and does not establish superiority. The evidence is limited by a small number of retrospective studies, heterogeneous reporting/outcome definitions, short follow-up, and potential selection bias. Multicenter studies with core lab-adjudicated outcomes are needed to investigate this topic further.

items.title: Subclinical cardiac autonomic and pulmonary dysfunction in ambulatory patients with cervicothoracic intradural spinal tumours: A prospective cross-sectional study.
items.abstract: Cervicothoracic intradural spinal tumours (C1-T12) may compromise autonomic and respiratory function due to proximity to sympathetic and cardiopulmonary regulatory centres. This study aimed to evaluate autonomic and pulmonary dysfunction in these patients using heart rate variability (HRV), autonomic function tests (AFTs), pulmonary function tests (PFTs), and echocardiography, with a subgroup analysis comparing intramedullary (IDIM) vs extramedullary (IDEM) conditions. In this prospective cross-sectional study, 68 ambulatory patients (mean age 36.9 ± 12.5 years; 30 male, 38 female) with radiologically confirmed cervicothoracic intradural tumours (Modified McCormick functional grades I-III) and 68 age- and gender-matched healthy, non-smoking controls, free of cardiopulmonary, neurological and endocrine disease and not taking medication, underwent preoperative heart rate variability (HRV) analysis, conventional autonomic function tests (AFT), pulmonary function tests (PFT) and echocardiography. Group comparisons used Student's t or Mann-Whitney U tests. Associations with functional grade were examined using Spearman correlation and chi-square tests. IDIM-IDEM comparisons were unadjusted and exploratory. Compared with controls, patients had lower SDNN (median 26.43 vs 40.01 ms; p = 0.0017), RMSSD (15.13 vs 31.96 ms; p < 0.0001), total power (695.7 vs 1335 ms2), low-frequency (LF) power (178.1 vs 369.1 ms2) and high-frequency (HF) power (106.4 vs 400.5 ms2), higher normalised LF with lower normalised HF, and a higher resting heart rate (84.93 vs 75.19 beats/min; p < 0.0001). Deep-breathing difference, Valsalva ratio, orthostatic heart-rate ratio and handgrip diastolic-pressure response were lower in patients (all p < 0.0001). Forced vital capacity and FEV1 (% predicted), inspiratory capacity, vital capacity, expiratory reserve volume and maximal voluntary ventilation were also lower. None of the HRV, AFT or PFT measures was significantly associated with Modified McCormick functional grade (all p ≥ 0.054). IDIM tumours spanned more vertebral segments than IDEM tumours (more than 3 segments in 56.4 % vs 24.1 %) and the groups differed in age. In unadjusted comparisons, resting heart rate was higher in IDIM tumours, whereas deep-breathing difference, handgrip response, FVC and ERV were lower in IDEM tumours. Ambulatory patients with cervicothoracic intradural spinal tumours demonstrated alterations in cardiac autonomic modulation and pulmonary function despite preserved ambulatory status and the absence of overt cardiopulmonary disease. The cross-sectional design shows associations, not causation. Differences between intramedullary and extramedullary tumours may reflect tumour compartment; they could also reflect differences in tumour level, extent and patient characteristics, and require confirmation in larger studies with adjusted analyses and longitudinal postoperative assessment.
