items.title: Impacts of traditional and industrial approaches to oil palm cultivation on bird biodiversity and conservation in a West African rainforest landscape.
items.abstract: Agricultural expansion threatens tropical ecosystems worldwide. Oil palm is cultivated primarily in Southeast Asia, but production in West Africa (its native range) is increasing rapidly. Here, oil palm is cultivated under traditional and industrial management, and the impacts on native West African ecosystems are poorly understood. Working within the framework of the Sustainable Oil Palm in West Africa (SOPWA) Project in Sinoe County, Liberia, we derived bird occurrence data using point count surveys across 54 plots in January-February 2023, spanning rainforest ('forest'), traditionally managed oil palm ('country palm'), and industrial oil palm systems, to investigate differences in bird species richness, community composition and community-level trait associations. Forest and country palm had comparable species richness, which was significantly higher than industrial oil palm. Taxonomic community composition differed across systems, with assemblages in country palm representing a mix of those in forest and industrial oil palm. Further, communities in forest and country palm were more associated with foraging in high strata, ant-associated behaviour, and an invertebrate diet. We detected four species of conservation concern in all systems, showing no consistent collective response to any specific system. Our findings show that country palm offers a promising option to preserve relatively high biodiversity as well as traditional cultivation practices in Liberia's managed landscape, although country palm is likely less productive than industrial oil palm. Oil palm systems are no replacement for rainforest ecosystems, and protection and designation of reserves and remnant forest patches are critical for wider bird conservation across West Africa.

items.title: Crystallinity-dependent dual role of iron oxides in regulating SOC mineralization and sequestration in paddy soil.
items.abstract: Improving soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration and reducing CO 2 emissions are essential for sustaining agricultural production in intensive farming regions worldwide. This study investigated the effect of iron oxide on SOC mineralization and sequestration in paddy soil because of its high redox reactivity and adsorption capacity. Soils were collected from an 11-year field experiment with two treatments: NPK fertilization and NPK fertilization combined with green manure (Chinese milk vetch) return. An incubation experiment was conducted with four treatments: no addition, 13 C-glucose, 13 C-glucose + low-crystallinity iron oxide (Fe 3 O 4 ), and 13 C-glucose + high-crystallinity iron oxide (α-Fe 2 O 3 ). Compared to the 13 C-glucose treatment, iron oxide addition reduced total CO 2 emissions by 3.5-10.0%, with the reduction being significant for α-Fe 2 O 3 . Source tracing revealed that soil-derived CO 2 decreased by 13-23% and 17-26% with Fe 3 O 4 and α-Fe 2 O 3 addition, respectively, while glucose-derived CO 2 increased by 26-45% and 12-48%. Both Fe 3 O 4 and α-Fe 2 O 3 induced a negative priming effect (-49 to -129 mg C kg -1 dry soil) and increased the 13 C content in SOC by 11.5-19.8%. The iron-bound carbon content was significantly increased by the iron oxide treatments, and its aromaticity was decreased by Fe 3 O 4 while increased by α-Fe 2 O 3 . This research concludes that iron oxides facilitate SOC sequestration by suppressing native SOC mineralization and promoting the storage of exogenous carbon, illustrating their potential role in improving soil fertility and enhancing environmental sustainability.

items.title: Setting the Pace of Epigenetic Aging in Mammals: A Hierarchy from Species to Individual.
items.abstract: Epigenetic clocks have transformed aging research by providing accurate molecular measures of biological age, but the factors regulating their pace across mammals remain unclear. This review proposes a hierarchy of regulation: species-level determinants that set intrinsic aging rate and lifespan, as well as individual-level modifiers acting within species. Comparative analyses show developmental tempo, rather than body mass, anchors species differences. Across individuals, caloric restriction and other perturbations of the insulin-like growth factor 1 nutrient-sensing axis alter epigenetic aging rate, whereas torpor models suggest body temperature, rather than metabolic rate per se, acts as the pacemaker. Gonadal hormones, reproduction, social environment, and ecology also contribute, with applications in livestock and wildlife conservation highlighted as means to capitalize on age-associated traits and exposures. Together, this work shows epigenetic clocks are far more than a yardstick for biological time; they reveal the multifaceted biology, and its hierarchy, that sets the pace of aging in mammals.

items.title: Sex Differences in Biological Responses: Mechanisms, Evolution, and Environmental Interactions.
items.abstract: Sex-specific phenotypes arise from complex interactions among genetic, epigenetic, hormonal, and environmental factors throughout development and across the lifespan. Although sex-determination mechanisms establish gonadal identity, they also initiate differences in sex-specific responses beyond reproductive tissues. Here, we review the diverse genetic and environmental sex-determination systems, highlighting how these mechanisms regulate sex-specific gene expression. We further examine the roles of hormones, epigenetic modifications, and environmental factors in shaping physiological, behavioral, and life-history differences between the sexes. Early-life conditions, social environments, and reproductive strategies further modify these trajectories, producing substantial within- and among-species variations in sex-specific phenotypes during development and aging. By integrating evidence across vertebrates and invertebrates, we propose a unified framework in which sex-specific phenotypes emerge from dynamic interactions between genomes, epigenomes, and environments. This comparative perspective discusses conserved and lineage-specific principles underlying the evolution, phenotypic plasticity, and adaptive significance of sex differences across diverse taxa.

items.title: Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants.
items.abstract: Humans and many other animals live in interconnected social communities that are essential for survival and well-being. In principle, communities can persist despite changes in constituent members. However, gradually accumulating changes to membership could push systems past critical thresholds into alternate states, restructuring patterns of connectivity. Such changes can further affect systemic resilience against disturbance. We investigated social network dynamics for 443 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years by tracking community membership and structure. Following accumulated demographic turnover, networks fractured into smaller and more isolated communities. Connections changed not only owing to loss of members but also modifications in relationships among remaining individuals. This provides empirical evidence of a persistent state change in the social network of a long-lived terrestrial mammal following gradually accumulating demographic turnover.

items.title: Transcriptomic characterization of obligate winter diapause in the emerald ash borer (Agrilus planipennis).
items.abstract: Wood-boring insects pose serious threats to trees, and even when living inside their hosts, they remain exposed to adverse conditions such as extreme low temperatures. Diapause is a critical strategy that enables certain pests to survive such environments and sustain their populations. Characterizing the molecular changes associated with diapause may therefore improve our understanding of their overwintering biology and environmental responses. However, transcriptomic studies of diapause in wood-boring insects remain relatively limited, partly because of their long life cycles, cryptic habits, and difficulties in sampling and observation. In this study, we focused on the emerald ash borer (EAB, Agrilus planipennis), an obligate diapausing pest that causes severe damage in both its native and invaded ranges. Using a comparative transcriptomic approach, we sequenced samples from three developmental stages: pre-diapause, diapause, and post-diapause. Compared to the other developmental stages, 1,147 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified as showing diapause-stage-associated expression patterns, with up-regulated genes outnumbering down-regulated genes by approximately 1.88-fold. By integrating exploratory GO/KEGG analyses, expression profiles, and previously reported diapause-associated pathways, we identified 47 candidate diapause-associated genes. Among these, 35 were upregulated (1.24- to 807.71-fold) and 12 were downregulated (0.04- to 0.74-fold) relative to the pre- and post-diapausing stages. KEGG Mapper further indicated that several candidates were associated with the Wnt, circadian rhythm, and FOXO signaling pathways. Collectively, these results characterize diapause-associated transcriptional changes in EAB and provide candidate genes and pathways for further investigation of overwintering responses in EAB and other winter-diapausing wood-boring insects.

items.title: Feeding type and microplastic particle concentration drive the ingestion of polystyrene beads in a natural zooplankton community.
items.abstract: The mismanagement of plastic waste in recent decades has led to global plastic pollution problem. Much of this plastic waste in the environment degrades into small particles, forming microplastics and increasing their abundance in ecosystems. These microplastics can be ingested by various microinvertebrates such as zooplankton. Using a microcosm experiment with a near-natural zooplankton community, we tested whether microplastics particle size and concentration affect the proportion of individuals ingesting polystyrene beads. Zooplankton were exposed to three bead sizes (1, 3, and 6 µm) at two concentrations (10 3 and 10 6 particles mL⁻ 1 ). Ingestion was assessed as the presence or absence of beads within individual organisms. As all beads sizes were within the ingestible range, the experiment was designed to evaluate size-dependent differences in ingestion probability rather than physical ingestion limit. At low concentrations, 40% of the cladocerans ingested microplastics, which was a higher percentage than copepods, rotifers and ostracods; suggesting that their unselective filter-feeding mode facilitates ingestion. At high microplastics concentrations, these were ingested by more than 70% of the organisms across all experimental groups, with only moderate differences in the proportion of individuals ingesting microplastics among rotifers, cladocerans, ostracods and copepods. These high percentages indicate that even raptorial feeders cannot avoid ingesting plastic at elevated concentrations. The size of the microplastics had no effect on their ingestibility. Overall, our near-natural experiment demonstrated that both feeding type and beads concentration significantly influenced microplastics ingestion by zooplankton.

items.title: Organization and remodeling of olfactory subsystems across development in the brilliant-thighed poison frog Allobates femoralis.
items.abstract: Olfaction is important for many ecological and social behaviors, but the development, organization, and molecular features of the olfactory system remain poorly understood in most anuran amphibians. Understanding developmental changes is particularly important because, during metamorphosis, the olfactory system must adapt to the very different conditions encountered by aquatic larvae and mainly terrestrial adults. In the brilliant-thighed poison frog Allobates femoralis, chemical cues influence behavior during both aquatic and terrestrial life stages, but the organization of its olfactory system has not yet been described. Here, we examined the anatomy and molecular features of the olfactory system of A. femoralis during development. We identified a main olfactory epithelium and a vomeronasal organ, together with a distinct buccal-exposed olfactory epithelium that is present only in larvae. We also found an additional larval sensory epithelium that is in close connection to the main olfactory epithelium. The different sensory epithelia showed distinct anatomical features and projected to defined regions of the main and accessory olfactory bulb. Immunohistochemistry revealed Gαo-expressing receptor neurons in all these epithelia, together with Gαo-positive axonal projections to the main and accessory olfactory bulb. Our study provides the first detailed description of the developing olfactory system of A. femoralis. These findings provide a basis for future studies linking the organization and function of the olfactory system to the olfaction-guided behaviors of this species.

items.title: Phylogenomic analysis of Dendrothele nivosa, a bark-inhabiting and host-specific crust fungus with an enigmatic ecological role.
items.abstract: Fungi in the genus Dendrothele (Basidiomycota, Russulales) are known for their obligate associations with the bark of living trees. However, the genus as it is currently defined is polyphyletic, and the phylogenetic placement and ecological roles of many of its species are poorly understood. We focused on Dendrothele nivosa , a common species in eastern North America associated with the bark of living Juniperus species. The taxonomic placement of D. nivosa has shifted among different orders and families since the 19th century. This species is found exclusively on the bark of living Juniperus , and its ecological niche remains unclear, as it is not associated with the bark of dead trees and thus may function as something other than a primary decomposer. Using Illumina short-read technology, we generated the first highquality genome assembly of D. nivosa (71 Mb length; BUSCO completeness of 97.5%, N50: 9572, L50: 1618). We determined its phylogenetic placement by building a whole genome-based phylogeny using publicly available data for the order Russulales. D. nivosa represents a distinct clade separate from its most closely related families, Bondarzewiaceae and Stereaceae. To better understand its ecological niche, we analyzed gene families of D. nivosa and closely related relatives, with an emphasis on carbohydrateassociated enzymes (CAZymes). The CAZyme profile in our assembly suggests that D. nivosa may function primarily as a bark/wood decay fungus, despite its exclusive association with living trees. In contrast to other close relatives, nearly half of the D. nivosa genome consists of transposable elements (TEs) caused by a massive invasion of long terminal repeat (LTR) retrotransposons, suggesting that TEs have played an important role in shaping D. nivosa 's evolution. The clarified phylogenetic position of D. nivosa and robust genomic data serve as a starting point for future work to determine the evolution and ecology of the diverse species of corticioid fungi associated with the bark of living trees.

items.title: Botulinum neurotoxin type a exposure and executive functioning: A multinational web-based survey.
items.abstract: Botulinum neurotoxin A (BoNT-A) injections have revolutionized both cosmetic and therapeutic interventions, gaining recognition for their positive physical and psychological effects. However, potential psychological correlates and safety concerns have received comparatively less attention. This cross-sectional study aimed to evaluate the association between BoNT-A exposure and executive function (EF) in a global sample. We collected data from participants across 155 countries using an online survey translated into 28 languages and distributed via web-based platforms. Chi-square tests and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) were employed to assess bivariate associations, while multivariable linear regression models using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) were employed to examine the association between BoNT-A exposure and EF scores, accounting for within-country clustering across the 155 countries while adjusting for sociodemographic and behavioral confounders. A total of 46,611 participants were screened, of whom 1,088 were excluded based on predefined criteria, leaving a primary eligible analytic cohort of N = 45,523. Among BoNT-A recipients, Self-Organization/Problem-Solving deficit scores varied significantly by injection frequency (p = 0.008), with the annual-injection group reporting a slightly higher mean score (42.3 ± 12.9), indicating a higher level of reported difficulties in this domain compared to other groups. However, the magnitude of this difference was small. No, clinically or statistically significant differences were observed across the remaining four executive function subscales (p > 0.05). In adjusted multivariable linear regression analysis controlling for sociodemographic and behavioral factors, BoNT-A injection was very small, albeit statistically significant, positive associations with higher scores for Self-Control/Inhibition (β = 0.508, 95% CI: 0.131-0.886, p = 0.008), self-regulation of emotion (β = 0.508, 95% CI: 0.238-0.778, p < 0.001), and Self-Motivation (β = 0.226, 95% CI: 0.023-0.428, p = 0.028), whereas no significant association was observed with Self-Organization/Problem-Solving, and self-management of time. Sensitivity analyses yielded a largely similar pattern across most domains but showed attenuation and loss of statistical significance for the Self-Organization/Problem-Solving association, highlighting domain-specific variability and the modest magnitude of the original estimate. These cross-sectional findings identify subtle, domain-specific observational associations. Because the Self-Organization/Problem-Solving association was attenuated in sensitivity analyses and residual confounding by indication is possible, these results should not be interpreted as evidence of toxin-induced neurocognitive changes or a causal effect. Prospective longitudinal cohort studies that incorporate comprehensive assessments of clinical indications and other potential confounders are warranted to further investigate these associations.

items.title: Internalized and Externalized Symptoms: A Qualitative Analysis of Discussion Threads from Femcel Forums.
items.abstract: The terms incels and femcels, respectively, designate men and women who identify as involuntary celibates. Incels and femcels share frustration linked to their inability to obtain love and sex, along with a deep sense of marginalization in their social, sexual, and romantic lives. Studies carried out on incels suggest the presence of internalizing and externalizing symptoms. However, because research on femcels is very limited, it is not known whether they encounter the same problems. The present study sought to fill this gap by identifying the types of internalizing and externalizing symptoms experienced by femcels, as observed in the forums where they voice themselves. A deductive content analysis of exchanges on two public forums where femcels post showed a high prevalence of internalizing symptoms. Most of these symptoms concerned loneliness, low self-esteem, depressed and anxious mood, and even suicidal ideation. Externalizing symptoms were far less frequent and mainly involved aggressive affects toward men. These findings echo those of Brix Rasmussen (2023), who reported that the dominant themes in femcel exchanges concerned their psychological distress, particularly depressive and anxious symptoms. They also highlight the need for future research on the psychological and relational difficulties associated with involuntary celibacy among women.

items.title: The first wave of macro-level nature connectedness research: Convergent insights and emerging directions.
items.abstract: The human-nature relationship is increasingly recognised as a fundamental driver of environmental issues. This article synthesises and reflects on an emerging "first wave" of quantitative macro-level research on nature connectedness, revealing how the human-nature relationship is shaped not only by individual experiences but by slow-moving cultural, socioeconomic, and historical forces. Drawing on multinational surveys, machine-learning analyses, and agent-based models spanning two centuries, the paper identifies consistent drivers of declining nature connectedness, including urbanisation, economic development, secularisation, and intergenerational transmission. It shows that these macro-factors explain both long-term declines and contemporary global variation, reframing nature connectedness as a societal property rather than an individual trait. This perspective paper synthesises these emergent insights, highlights the conceptual foundations of an integrated science of nature connectedness, and outlines priorities for future research into systemic, multi-level interventions capable of informing policy and societal transformation of the human-nature relationship.

items.title: Norms for gender-inclusive role nouns in Italian: The GIRN-I database.
items.abstract: Understanding how linguistic alternatives to gender-binary forms are perceived is particularly relevant in languages that encode gendered categorisations through specific linguistic markers, such as Italian. Indeed, gender-diverse individuals face additional distress associated with perceived invisibility arising from the absence of adequate linguistic forms. To date, substantial research has been devoted to identifying demographic and socio-political factors underlying preferences for gender-inclusive language. However, far less is known about the cognitive mechanisms that underlie these attitudes. Here, we provide the first Italian psycholinguistic database of role nouns (e.g., nurse, carpenter, teacher) encompassing both gendered (i.e., feminine and masculine) and gender-inclusive (i.e., asterisk and schwa) desinences. Remarkably, this is the first contribution explicitly assessing Italian participants' dispositions towards gender-inclusive desinences. We asked participants to rate role nouns on nine semantic dimensions, including classic dimensions like familiarity and sensibility and less conventional ones like psychological distance and political relevance. Our findings suggest no clear preference for either of the two inclusive alternatives, both of which are perceived as less familiar and less pleasant than their corresponding gendered forms. We suggest that processing components related to linguistic fluency may also contribute to explaining observed preference patterns. Taken together, our findings underscore the importance of considering semantic and linguistic processing factors, alongside ideological and social variables, when investigating attitudes towards gender-inclusive language.

items.title: A practical guide to self-organising maps in psychological research.
items.abstract: Identifying shared and distinct profiles, whether of symptoms, personality traits, or cognitive abilities, is essential for understanding psychological phenomena, yet doing so requires navigating interrelated theoretical, conceptual, and technical complexities. First, most psychological phenomena typically exist along continuous spectra rather than discrete categories, complicating the characterisation of inherently heterogeneous constructs. Second, studying individual differences requires balancing population-level generalisation with person-level interpretability, which is critical for applied science and clinical practice. Third, psychological data often contain missing values, non-linear relationships, and high-dimensional patterns that violate standard statistical assumptions. Commonly used approaches for profile detection often fall short of these demands, producing oversimplified or difficult-to-interpret results that are hard to map back to the individual. In contrast, self-organising maps (SOMs) offer a powerful, visual, and intuitive solution that addresses these challenges. Despite growing interest, SOMs remain underutilised in psychology, likely due to a lack of accessible tutorials and clear guidelines tailored to the field. This tutorial introduces SOMs to psychologists without technical backgrounds, emphasising practical implementation. We provide evidence-based recommendations for key methodological decisions, accompanied by annotated R code. Using a dataset of depressive symptoms as an illustrative case, we present a complete workflow covering data preprocessing, map initialisation, parameter optimisation, and interpretation. We further discuss advanced SOM extensions relevant to psychological research and highlight key limitations of the method. By making SOMs accessible, this tutorial supports nuanced, person-centred analyses that preserve the complexity of psychological phenomena.

items.title: Aphantasia in Healthy Relationships: Visual Imagery in Attachment styles, Dyadic bonding, Social Networks & Loneliness.
items.abstract: This study explores the role of mental imagery in relationship functioning, attachment styles, loneliness and social networks, with a focus on individuals with aphantasia-a rare trait characterised by weak or absent mental imagery. We compared 82 participants (44 with aphantasia and 38 without) using psychological scales including the State Adult Attachment Measure, Experiences in Close Relationships-Revised scale, UCLA Loneliness Scale, Social Network Index, Dyadic Adjustment Scale, and Dyadic Coping Inventory. Results revealed that individuals with aphantasia reported significantly lower anxious attachment compared to controls, supporting the notion that lower mental imagery offers a protective effect against relationship anxiety. There were no penalties for aphantasics in the size of their social networks, in secure and avoidant attachment, or in dyadic adjustment within romantic relationships (with evidence to support these null effects). This suggests no necessary role for imagery in these domains, and/or compensatory mechanisms employed by aphantasics. Finally, we also investigated loneliness, network diversity and dyadic coping under stress but found insufficient evidence to draw conclusions. Overall our findings challenge assumptions about the universality of mental imagery in social and romantic relationship social processes, highlighting the variability of human cognition. Our study also contributes to understanding the cognitive and emotional nuances of aphantasia, with implications for therapeutic practices that consider individual imagery differences.

items.title: Cue modality modulates dynamic functional network organization during motor imagery: Evidence from EEG functional connectivity and spatiotemporal decoding.
items.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) is typically guided by external sensory cues; however, how cue modality and imagery type jointly influence functional connectivity during post-cue MI remains unclear. This study combined functional connectivity analysis with a CNN-TemporalConv-MLP spatiotemporal decoding model to investigate phase-locking value (PLV) differences across visual versus auditory cues and kinesthetic (KMI) versus visual (VMI) motor imagery. Functional connectivity analyses revealed that all connections with significant cue-modality effects in the early theta band showed higher PLV following visual cues. In the beta band, PLV was higher under visual cues in the earlier significant time window, whereas it was higher under auditory cues in the later significant time window. In contrast, differences between KMI and VMI were primarily localized to connections in the theta and alpha bands, while interactions between cue modality and imagery type emerged selectively in the theta, beta, and gamma bands. Decoding analyses showed that PLV functional connectivity features contained discriminative information about both factors. Overall cue-modality decoding achieved moderate performance, and performance improved when KMI and VMI conditions were held constant. By contrast, overall imagery-type classification showed relatively low discriminability. However, KMI versus VMI classification improved within specific cueing backgrounds, with better performance under fixed visual or auditory cues than under mixed cue-modality conditions. These findings indicate that the influence of cue modality can extend into subsequent MI, with functional connectivity differences showing selectivity across time, frequency, and connections. Condition-related differences were evident in both connection-specific PLV effects and deep learning decoding of PLV features.

items.title: Stimulus prior and reward probability differentially affect response bias in perceptual decision making.
items.abstract: Signal detection theory posits that subjects in two-stimulus, two-choice discrimination tasks decide by comparing random samples of an evidence variable to a static decision criterion. While the core assumptions of the theory have received ample experimental support, it has become evident that the decision criterion is not static but subject to trial-by-trial fluctuations and can be influenced by experimental manipulations. The mechanisms governing the trial-by-trial criterion changes are however not well understood. Here, we report results from five experiments in which we subjected rats to a two-stimulus, two-choice auditory discrimination task. In the first three experiments, we investigated the effects of stimulus presentation ratios and reward ratios and provide clear evidence that the effects of changing reward ratios are more pronounced than those of stimulus presentation ratios. A model-based analysis revealed that this effect was due to more than tenfold higher learning rates when reward ratios were manipulated. In two separate experiments, we investigated the effect of reward density (i.e., global reward rate) on criterion learning but failed to find consistent effects. A systematic comparison of three different trial-by-trial criterion learning models based on detection theory, the matching law, and reinforcement learning showed that no model was able to capture the differential effects of stimulus presentation and reward ratios. We conclude that subjects explicitly represent either prior stimulus probabilities or entire stimulus distributions, and accordingly future models need to represent these factors as well.

items.title: Ask, don't assume: Editorial and Data Integrity Triage (EDIT), an editor's practice-based checklist for screening manuscripts at submission.
items.abstract: As an editor, I regularly find problems in submitted manuscripts that need explaining before peer review can begin. A reference cannot be found, participant numbers in the abstract differ from those in the tables, or the methods do not explain the results. Most have an honest explanation, but some do not, and paper mills and text produced by artificial intelligence (AI) add to the pressure on editors. My message in this paper is simple. When something does not add up, editors should ask the authors a specific question before assuming anything, and they should judge the work itself and leave aside who wrote it. I describe Editorial and Data Integrity Triage (EDIT), a checklist I developed from my editorial work at the Journal of Hospital Infection and from academic integrity practice. EDIT has 20 checks in five domains covering reporting, methods and data, references, authorship and declarations, and submission files. Ten core checks can be applied to every submission and the others when they are relevant. Each finding leads to routine handling, a request for clarification or a pause for senior assessment. Writing style, a free email account, an incomplete author profile, the authors' country and unusually tidy data are not treated as evidence of a problem. A fictional example follows one submission from the first checks to an editorial decision, and I identify the checks that peer reviewers can use. EDIT reflects one editor's practice, and independent review and testing are needed before it is used routinely.

items.title: Childhood coercive control and suicide: An under-recognised pathway via entrapment.
items.abstract: Childhood experiences of domestic violence (also referred to as domestic abuse, in the context of parental intimate partner violence/abuse) is a well-established risk factor for adverse mental health outcomes, including suicidality. However, dominant measurement approaches continue to prioritise discrete incidents of physical violence, obscuring coercive control as a pervasive and chronic pattern of harm. This narrow framing limits understanding of how children's experiences of parental domestic violence create risk for suicide. This article reconceptualises childhood experiences of coercive control as a distinct and underexamined risk factor for suicidality. We advance the understanding of entrapment as a central mechanism through which coercive control may contribute to suicidality and identify critical gaps in current evidence and measurement approaches. Coercive control operates across the family unit and frequently persists following parental separation, creating developmental environments characterised by chronic fear, enforced dependency, and constrained autonomy. We argue that these conditions may give rise to a sustained sense of entrapment, a risk factor for suicidality, positioning childhood experiences of coercive control as an under-recognised pathway to suicide-related outcomes among children and young people. Childhood experiences of coercive control are inadequately measured in research, with suicidality largely overlooked as an outcome, obscuring the true extent and impact of the problem. Better pattern-based measurement and recognition across research, clinical practice and family courts could improve identification of abuse and strengthen safeguarding.

items.title: Disruptions in mentalizing trauma across the prenatal and postnatal periods: Stability and associations with environmental stressors and infant development.
items.abstract: Disruptions in trauma-specific reflective functioning (T-RF) among parents are linked to poorer mental health and parental functioning, whereas effective T-RF is a key protective factor. However, the natural trajectory of T-RF and its association with infant development remain unclear. This longitudinal study examined trait- and state-like features of disruptions in T-RF from pregnancy to postpartum, and its associations with infant development. A sample of 185 pregnant women were recruited during the second trimester (T1) and followed up in the third trimester (T2), as well as between five and 14 months postpartum (T3). Self-report questionnaires were used to assess T-RF at all three time points and stressful life events and infant development at T3. Latent growth curve analyses showed significant interindividual variability at baseline (M = 22.82, p < 0.001; s2 = 135.59, p < 0.001), but overall stability across time (M = -0.33, p = 0.49; s2 = 6.40, p = 0.57), supporting its trait-like features. Greater exposure to prenatal stressful life events was associated with greater prenatal disruptions in T-RF (β = 0.17, p = 0.03), a finding that is consistent with, but does not establish, the possibility that T-RF may exhibit state-like characteristic. Higher disruptions in prenatal T-RF prospectively predicted infant developmental difficulties (β = -0.23, p = 0.01). This study suggests that T-RF primarily reflects stable individual differences and is associated with infant development. Future research should examine whether enhancing prenatal T-RF through psychological interventions can promote infant development.

items.title: Family Structure Theory: Understanding the Role of Childhood Household Composition on Life Outcomes.
items.abstract: Family Structure Theory (FST) provides a conceptual framework for understanding the higher rate of incarceration observed in children from single-mother families without significant co-parenting arrangements, or extended and multigenerational family support. Persistent inequities have been observed in social, financial, educational, legal, and health outcomes amongst this cohort compared to their two-or-more caregiver peers. Empirical research consistently demonstrates that, on average, children nurtured in this context suffer more disadvantaged outcomes than their peers, yet traditional explanations-such as socioeconomic deprivation, parental education, historical oppression, and current systemic discrimination-fail to fully account for the observed differences after adjustment. FST posits that household composition exerts an independent and measurable effect on child development, functioning as an independent determinant rather than merely a correlate. Drawing upon interdisciplinary evidence from sociology, developmental psychology, public health, criminology, and public policy, the theory identifies three principal pathways - time and attention, economic resources, and social capital -through which family structure shapes lifelong trajectories. Importantly, these mechanisms operate beyond traditional socioeconomic, structural, and environmental variables, suggesting that interventions must address more than material deprivation or location of habitation. FST underscores the importance of replicating or substituting the protective and developmental functions of multi-caregiver households in social programs targeting single-mother families. By centering the family unit as a foundational determinant of measurable outcomes, Family Structure Theory provides a more comprehensive model for explaining life course disparities and guiding future policy, research, and interventions designed to help remove these inequities.

items.title: Investigating 24-Hour Movement Behaviors in Young People With Learning Disabilities: Protocol for a Mixed Methods Study.
items.abstract: Background Physical activity (PA), sedentary behavior (SB), and sleep play a key role in the health and development of young people. This has led to the development of guidelines on PA, SB, and sleep for children and young people aged 5 to 17 years. Adherence to these integrated guidelines is associated with favorable physical, mental, and cognitive health outcomes. However, evidence regarding 24-hour movement behaviors (MBs) among young people with learning disabilities is scarce, particularly in the United Kingdom, where no studies have comprehensively examined adherence to all guideline components or explored the factors influencing these behaviors in this population. Objective This study aims to investigate 24-hour MBs among young people with learning disabilities in Scotland, United Kingdom; determine adherence to PA, SB, screen time, and sleep recommendations; assess the feasibility and acceptability of measuring 24-hour MBs in this population; and explore individual, social, and environmental barriers to and facilitators of MBs. Methods This mixed methods study recruited young people aged 11 to 17 years who attended secondary schools for children with additional support needs (ASN) in Scotland. Participants were asked to wear an ActiGraph GT3X accelerometer continuously for 7 consecutive days to objectively assess PA, SB, and sleep. Parent- and youth-completed diaries captured sleep schedules, screen time, and monitored nonwear periods. Individualized activity profiles were produced to summarize participants' daily MBs and support engagement in the qualitative phase. A purposive subsample participated in semistructured interviews exploring experiences, barriers, and facilitators associated with MBs. Quantitative data will be analyzed descriptively to determine MB patterns and guideline adherence, while qualitative data will undergo thematic analysis informed by the capability, opportunity, and motivation-behavior (COM-B) model, the theoretical domains framework and the behavior change wheel. Results The study was funded by the Baily Thomas Charitable Fund from April 2025 to July 2026. Ethics approval was granted by the University of Strathclyde Ethics Committee (UEC25/10). Recruitment and data collection were completed in June 2026 across participating ASN schools in Scotland. This manuscript describes the study protocol and planned analyses; however, data cleaning and analysis were ongoing at the time of submission. Quantitative and qualitative findings are expected to be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and conference presentations during 2027. Conclusions This study is among the first in the United Kingdom to comprehensively examine all components of the 24-hour MB framework in young people with learning disabilities using objective measurement and qualitative inquiry. The findings will provide important evidence on MB patterns, guideline adherence, and modifiable determinants of behavior, informing the development of theory-informed, inclusive interventions designed to improve health and well-being among young people with learning disabilities. items.title: Mobile Health Apps for Individuals Who Are Blind or Have Low Vision: Systematic Review of Evidence, Accessibility, and App Quality.
items.abstract: Background Individuals who are blind or have low vision experience disproportionate burdens in both physical and psychological functioning, and mobile health apps may help address some of these needs. However, their availability, accessibility, and empirical support for this population remain unclear. Objective This systematic review aimed to identify mobile health apps relevant to supporting physical and psychological functioning in individuals who are blind or have low vision, summarize the empirical evidence available for these apps, and examine their accessibility and quality. Methods We used a multicomponent approach that combined (1) identification of apps through organizational recommendations; (2) a systematic search of the scientific literature, conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines; and (3) an exploratory accessibility and app quality appraisal using the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 and the Mobile App Development and Assessment Guide. Results A total of 19 unique mobile health apps were identified after combining and deduplicating apps identified through organizational recommendations and scientific literature. Fifteen apps were identified through organizational recommendations, and 14 empirical studies evaluating 11 apps were included in the qualitative synthesis. Only a subset of these studies specifically involved blind or low-vision participants; several evaluated apps in broader clinical or general populations where visual impairment status was not reported. The identified apps focused primarily on physical functioning, particularly medication management, glucose monitoring, pharmaceutical information access, and health care access. No apps primarily designed to support psychological functioning in individuals who are blind or have low vision were identified. Of 14 studies, 6 (43%) were rated as being of good methodological quality. The exploratory user-informed accessibility appraisal showed variability across apps: MyPills received the most favorable accessibility profile, with "High" ratings across all 4 Web Content Accessibility Guidelines principles, whereas several organizationally recommended apps received low ratings across most principles. Mobile App Development and Assessment Guide scores ranged from 8/39 to 34/39, with Medisafe scoring highest. Conclusions The current landscape of mobile health apps for individuals who are blind or have low vision remains limited, uneven in accessibility and quality, and supported by a limited and heterogeneous evidence base. The absence of identified apps targeting psychological functioning represents a particularly important gap. Improving the development and implementation of mobile health apps for individuals who are blind or have low vision will require more than increasing the number of available apps; it will require apps that are accessible from the outset, rigorously evaluated, and developed with the people they are intended to serve.

items.title: Text Psychometrics: Assessing psychological constructs in text using natural language processing.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing (NLP). Yet when used to assess psychological constructs in text, they are generally not evaluated for the types of validity, reliability, and standardization typically expected from traditional questionnaires with rating scales. This study bridges that gap by proposing a framework for evaluating the psychometric properties of NLP-based psychological assessments (including LLMs-based ones), an area of research we refer to as Text Psychometrics. We first review different NLP methods, compare their ability to address key challenges in psychological research such as explainability, and outline ways of evaluating them on many desirable psychometric properties. Our goal is to describe most psychometric properties that may be of interest, especially for psychology and NLP researchers who are less familiar with psychometrics or psychometricians who are less familiar with NLP. We then illustrate the tradeoffs of different NLP methods through two empirical studies. Study 1 classifies thousands of crisis counseling conversations and Reddit posts into different types of mental health issues and introduces a novel method to evaluate text models for content validity-the extent to which a test captures the full range of expressions of a single construct. Study 2 examines prospective criterion validity by estimating how 49 known suicide risk factors predict imminent risk in crisis counseling conversations. We find that mentioning lethal means for suicide, the police, depressed mood, and anxiety in text as well as the texter writing more than the counselor characterize the conversations that end up needing an emergency service intervention for imminent suicide risk, which showcases the interpretability of the method that was used. In sum, NLP studies in psychology often rely on only a few validation metrics; here, we demonstrate the need for broader psychometric evaluation and, as a step towards Text Psychometrics, provide practical examples and future directions that can help researchers evaluate these models.

items.title: Cultural variability in the link between affect and meaning in life: Evidence from 69 countries.
items.abstract: People tend to evaluate their lives as more meaningful when they experience more positive affect and less negative affect. However, most evidence for this association comes from Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic societies, which are culturally distinctive in their strong emphasis on happiness. To assess the cross-cultural generality of the affect-meaning link, we conducted the largest cross-cultural investigation of this association to date. Between 2022 and 2024, we collected data from 18,672 individuals across 69 countries spanning all inhabited continents. Across cultures, the association between affect and meaning was largely robust: Positive affect was positively related to meaning in life in 62 countries, and negative affect was negatively related to meaning in 57 countries. At the same time, substantial cross-cultural variation emerged. Multilevel analyses indicated that both associations were, on average, somewhat stronger in Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic countries than in most other regions. Moreover, a cross-level interaction showed that the links between affect (both positive and negative) and meaning were stronger in countries that more strongly idealize happiness, even after accounting for national differences in wealth, religiosity, and life satisfaction. Cross-cultural differences were more pronounced for the association between negative affect and meaning than for the association involving positive affect. Meaning was consistently associated with all eight discrete emotions. However, cultural valuation of happiness moderated only the associations with fear, shame, sadness, anger, and gratitude, with weaker evidence for relaxedness and excitement and no moderation observed for love. Together, these findings suggest that while affective experiences are a widespread basis for evaluating meaning in life, their psychological significance is amplified in Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic cultural contexts that place greater emphasis on happiness. items.title: Emotional reactivity, emotion perception, and emotional empathy.
items.abstract: Neuropsychological models of emotion posit that we simulate the feelings of others in ourselves as a means to understand them. Accordingly, people who are more emotionally reactive may be better at simulation and responding to the emotions of others. This study aimed to examine the relationship between emotional responsivity and emotion perception in normal adults and to determine whether these factors change with age. A trait measure of emotional reactivity (Perth Emotional Reactivity Scale), a naturalistic video measure of emotion perception (Complex Audio-Visual Emotion Assessment Task-Short), and a trait measure of emotional empathy (Balanced Emotional Empathy Scale) were administered to 369 normal healthy adults 24-83 years of age using a digital research platform. People high in negative reactivity (and low in positive reactivity) were more accurate recognizing negative emotional expressions (small to medium effects: r = -.130 to -.203). People high in positive reactivity tended to self-report greater emotional empathy (r = .441-.443). There were no differences across age groups, although there was an indication that older adults self-reported fewer negative mood states (Depression Anxiety Stress Scale). We found a relationship between responsivity and emotion perception, consistent with the simulation model of emotion processing, but specifically for negative reactivity. The results suggest that high positive reactivity, likely reflecting good emotion regulation, is aligned with empathy. Older adults do not show a decrement if we use naturalistic video materials to assess emotion perception. These findings require replication in a more culturally diverse sample but have interesting implications for rehabilitation. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: A systematic investigation of age-gender intersectional stereotypes and their consequences.
items.abstract: Research on age and gender stereotypes has largely examined these dimensions in isolation or reduced their intersection to broad perceptions of warmth and competence. To foster a more nuanced understanding of age-gender intersecting stereotypes, the present research offers a systematic, inductive-deductive investigation of stereotype content toward individuals with intersecting age and gender identities. Using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, Study 1 inductively develops and validates six target-specific stereotype measurement models comprising 22 stereotype dimensions capturing mixed-valence content of younger, middle-aged, and older women and men. Study 2 uses a deductive approach to categorize these dimensions into a framework distinguishing interactive, additive, age-based, and gender-based stereotypes, with multiple interactive or additive stereotypes emerging for each age-gender target. Study 3 establishes the convergent and discriminant validity of these dimensions and finds evidence that some dimensions predict attitudes beyond established models of person perception. Finally, Study 4 demonstrates that age-gender targets are differentially assigned to organizational roles that align with stereotype content associated with their groups and that role-relevant stereotype dimensions predict hiring decisions beyond broader perceptions of warmth and competence. Overall, the present studies highlight the complex interplay between age and gender in shaping stereotype content, show the consequences of these stereotypes in real-world contexts, contribute to ongoing social-psychological arguments for going beyond warmth and competence in stereotype models, and ultimately, lay essential groundwork for further empirical investigations on an increasingly timely topic. items.title: Navigating divorce and partner bereavement: Personality and trajectories of change in life satisfaction and mental health.
items.abstract: Dissolutions of romantic relationships can elicit diverse reactions across various aspects of well-being, but they also offer an opportunity to examine which factors promote resilience and identify individuals at risk. In this preregistered multisample longitudinal study, we examined the heterogeneity in life satisfaction and mental health changes around and during divorce or partner bereavement and whether personality (i.e., traits and resilient vs. nonresilient personality profiles) may explain individual differences in change trajectories. Data from 1,306 divorcees and 1,150 bereaved partners were drawn from nationally representative panel studies in the Netherlands (N = 12,551), Germany (N = 10,830), and China (N = 28,628) and analyzed using growth mixture modeling. Four life satisfaction trajectories and three mental health trajectories were identified for each event. Recovery and resilience emerged as the most common trajectories across events, outcomes, and samples. Among personality factors, neuroticism was the most consistent predictor of a lower likelihood of belonging to a resilience trajectory. This study advanced the generalizability of findings across diverse loss-based events, populations, and aspects of well-being. The findings further underscore the influence of neuroticism in shaping, and potentially complicating, psychological adjustment surrounding divorce and partner bereavement. items.title: The structure and history of English words that describe people.
items.abstract: The English language is filled with words that are used to describe people, such as "nice," "skilled," "conservative," and "attractive." This broad trait space includes words that describe personality but also words that describe people's physical, sociodemographic, and ideological differences. Here we define trait space as the sum of stable, comparative, and socially meaningful descriptors and map this space by combining large language models, human ratings, and historical text analyses. Across four studies, we (a) introduce a comprehensive trait list (2,847 trait words); (b) establish normative human ratings of these words (3,070 English speakers) along 24 dimensions drawn from prior literature; (c) identify a four-factor structure of fitness, agency, communion, and traditionalism from these dimensions, which covers 95.4% of trait words; and (d) reveal systematic differences in the coherence, valence, and evolution of these factors. Specifically, these four factors differ in their coherence (e.g., communion is the most semantically coherent while traditionalism the least), valence (e.g., communion and agency show more alignment between their semantic direction and valence than traditionalism and fitness; communion has more negative words while agency and traditionalism more positive ones), and historical usage (e.g., fitness and communion are older than traditionalism; communion is converging in semantic space while agency diverging). These findings showcase new large language model-based methods for discovering and analyzing trait words. We close by motivating a functional constructionist view: The meaning, structure, and use of traits constitute a culturally constructed toolkit that represents socially relevant individual differences to help navigate recurring interaction problems. items.title: Understanding the impact of racism in Canada using the Racial Trauma Scale.
items.abstract: Equitable and inclusive mental health care requires the ability to identify/measure symptoms to inform client diagnosis and care, regardless of race. Yet, due to unfamiliarity, a skills deficit, discomfort, and an absence of appropriate tools, many clinicians fail to identify racial trauma. The Racial Trauma Scale (RTS) is a novel self-assessment measure for quantifying distress symptoms due to racism. Using the RTS, this study aimed to understand the impact of racial trauma among racialized individuals residing in Canada. A sample of 756 racially diverse participants from across Canada completed a battery of measures, RTS included, to establish the validity of the scale and better understand racial trauma in racialized Canadians. RTS scores were positively correlated (large effect) with measures of depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress disorder, and posttraumatic cognitions. Reliability was excellent in both English and French versions of the scale (Cronbach α = .98) and in the nine-item short version (α = .95 and α = .93, respectively). Among racialized groups, racial trauma severity was highest in Black (M = 62.11; SD = 23.19) and lowest in Asian respondents (M = 51.32; SD = 22.04). White respondents reported notably lower racial trauma severity (M = 36.36; SD = 15.16). There were also significant differences in RTS scores across provinces, with the highest scores in the Atlantic region. Findings indicate that clinicians can use the RTS to identify racism-related distress and symptoms to target for intervention. Results highlight the need for culturally informed assessment and intervention of this prevalent and debilitating condition. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Life satisfaction and motives for postponing parenthood among Polish women: A sequential indirect association model of depressive symptoms, future anxiety, and procrastination.
items.abstract: Postponed parenthood is an increasingly common feature of reproductive patterns in high- and middle-income societies. Although previous research has examined factors associated with delayed parenthood, less is known about the psychological characteristics linked to self-reported motives for postponement. The present study examined the relationship between life satisfaction and motives for postponing parenthood and tested a theoretically ordered cross-sectional model involving depressive symptoms, future anxiety, and procrastination. Participants were 201 childless Polish women aged 20-44 years (M = 32.75, SD = 6.91). They completed the Satisfaction with Life Scale, the Multidimensional Scale of Motives for Postponing Parenthood, the Brief Screen for Depression, the Dark Future Scale, and the Pure Procrastination Scale. Higher life satisfaction was negatively related to some, but not all, motive-specific outcomes and to depressive symptoms. Depressive symptoms were positively associated with future anxiety, which was, in turn, positively related to procrastination. Higher procrastination was linked to higher motive-specific and overall postponement scores. The hypothesized specific sequential indirect association of life satisfaction with motives through depressive symptoms, future anxiety, and procrastination was statistically supported for uncertainty and incompetence (B = -.0083, 95% bootstrap CI [-.0214, - .0007]), fear of change (B = -.0054, 95% bootstrap CI [-.0148, - .0003]), financial security concern (B = -.0095, 95% bootstrap CI [-.0229, - .0012]), and the overall motives score (B = -.0324, 95% bootstrap CI [-.0818, - .0027]). The corresponding sequential indirect associations were not supported for self-focus, parenthood as a burden, or worry about a child's future, indicating that the pattern differed across motives. Sensitivity analyses indicated that some outcome-specific sequential associations were not robust to the exclusion of potential multivariate outliers. Overall, the findings suggest that life satisfaction, depressive symptoms, future anxiety, and procrastination show distinct associations with self-reported reasons for postponing parenthood. Given the cross-sectional design, the observed sequential indirect associations should not be interpreted as evidence of temporal or causal psychological mechanisms.

items.title: Health Literacy of Mental Health Workers: A Latent Profile Analysis.
items.abstract: Low health literacy is linked to poorer outcomes. Individuals with mental illness often have lower health literacy and engage in less healthy behaviours. Healthcare workers play an important role in supporting consumers' health literacy, but they may also have gaps in their own health literacy skills. This study aims to (a) explore the multidimensional health literacy profiles of mental health workers, (b) compare their health literacy to the Australian general population and (c) examine health behaviours within health literacy profiles. Participants were 338 mental health workers employed at an Australian community-based mental health treatment service. Multidimensional health literacy was measured using the Health Literacy Questionnaire. Latent profile analysis was used to identify multidimensional health literacy profiles. Three health literacy profiles were identified: lowest (23%), moderate (65%) and highest (12%). Workers in the lowest health literacy profile had significantly lower health literacy compared with the general population of Australia and were less likely to engage in physical activity and consume vegetables. Improving the health literacy of workers could improve their well-being and promote healthier behaviours among consumers. Workers with lower health literacy would benefit from greater support from education providers, services and the wider system prioritising health literacy improvements and training.

items.title: What makes people seeking asylum and refugees well? A qualitative scoping review using an asset-based approach.
items.abstract: People seeking asylum and with refugee status (ASR) often face worse health outcomes compared to host populations. Despite this, ASR are underserved in healthcare and research, resulting in a knowledge gap about what promotes their health and resilience. The aim of this review is to define what ASR communities express makes them well despite adversity by looking at the assets of individuals and communities identified in community-based research. A scoping review of peer-reviewed papers and grey literature documenting patient-centred holistic health, wellbeing and social outcomes in community-based research with ASR. In total, 24 papers met the inclusion criteria. Wellbeing was primarily defined by safety, empowerment and a sense of purpose. Three things matter most for wellbeing: gaining knowledge and skills (like language and education), having meaningful things to do (like work or volunteering) and access to connections you care deeply about (like family, culture and faith). The study demonstrates that wellbeing for ASR is multifaceted, encompassing psychological, social and cultural dimensions. Asset-based approaches support holistic wellbeing in underserved populations by shifting the focus from identifying problems and deficits to recognising and building upon strengths, capabilities and existing resources. Although there are challenges in measurement, qualitative and participatory research approaches are proving effective in capturing the complex needs and outcomes for this population.

items.title: Prevalence and Determinants of Underweight Among Children Aged 6-10 Years in Urban and Rural Areas of Central Ethiopia: A Community-Based Comparative Cross-Sectional Study.
items.abstract: ObjectivesThe evidence revealed that underweight is a major public health concern affecting school-aged children in low and middle-income countries, including Ethiopia. Underweight affects children aged 6-10 years, growth and development, which leads to poor physical, cognitive, and social performance. Thus, this study aimed to assess the prevalence and determinants of underweight among children aged 6-10 years old in urban and rural areas of Central Ethiopia.MethodsA community-based comparative cross-sectional study was conducted among 541 children from January 2 to May 2, 2023. Participants were selected using simple random sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and anthropometric measurements. Children's nutritional status was assessed using weight-for-age z-scores calculated with WHO AnthroPlus software. Factors associated with underweight were identified using binary logistic regression analysis. Statistical significance was declared at p < 0.05, and associations were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).ResultsIn this study, 501 children were enrolled, yielding a response rate of 92.6%. Underweight was more common in rural areas than in urban areas, with prevalence rates of 24.9% (95% CI: 21.2, 26.3) and 17.5% (95% CI: 14.0, 19.0), respectively. Among urban children, maternal age at first birth (AOR = 4.4; 95% CI: 1.63, 12.2), handwashing after latrine use (AOR = 0.16; 95% CI: 0.12, 0.46), use of treated drinking water (AOR = 0.20; 95% CI: 0.18, 0.51), and family planning use (AOR = 0.12; 95% CI: 0.10, 0.47) were determinants of underweight. In contrast, among rural children, maternal age at first birth (AOR = 2.4; 95% CI: 1.34, 8.91), no antenatal care (ANC) follow-up (AOR = 2.3; 95% CI: 1.27, 6.53), diarrhea in the previous month (AOR = 2.8; 95% CI: 1.63, 9.35), dietary diversity (AOR = 6.0; 95% CI: 2.79, 13.2), and a history of illness in the preceding two weeks (AOR = 3.4; 95% CI: 1.91, 7.23) were identified as determinants of underweight.ConclusionUnderweight was more prevalent among rural children (24.9%) than among urban children (17.5%), highlighting the need for context-specific nutritional interventions. Interventions addressing the identified factors should be strengthened to improve the nutritional status of school-age children in both rural and urban settings.

items.title: Suicide Among Indigenous Peoples in Brazil: Ecological Study and Geospatial Mapping of Cases, 2013-2022.
items.abstract: This retrospective ecological study analyzes the temporal trend of suicides among Indigenous men and women in Brazilian cities between 2013 and 2022. Suicide mortality data were obtained from the Ministry of Health's Mortality Information System (Sistema de Informações sobre Mortalidade, SIM). Records were classified according to the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10), focusing on intentional self-harm (X60-X84). There was a significant increase in suicides among Indigenous men (41%) and women (42.9%). The highest absolute numbers occurred in the North, for men (n = 547) and women (n = 195). The Central-West showed the highest suicide rates for men (30.5/100,000) and women (8.8/100,000). The most affected age group among men was 20-29 years (37.3%), while among women it was 15-19 years (36%). Findings highlight the urgency of suicide prevention public policies for Indigenous peoples, particularly youth and young adults. Investment in culturally sensitive mental health strategies is essential to address Indigenous community contexts and expand access to psychosocial support services.

items.title: The anti-misinformation movement must not become anti-science.
items.abstract: Communities of experts have an indispensable role to play in addressing misinformation. However, some of these efforts have weaponized the term "misinformation" to suppress dissenting viewpoints, risking inadvertently turning the anti-misinformation movement into an anti-science one. The scientific community should instead be asking: how can we cultivate forums that promote discourse according to scientific values and incentivize broad participation in them? Here, we diagnose this problem and propose a number of remedies. Operationalizing precise definitions of misinformation can help curate information in public forums. Certification of trusted organizations by scientific societies can help ensure trustworthy information is incorporated and up-ranked in AI and search algorithms. Professional societies can champion shared principles of scientific debate in public with clear, transparent professional guidelines. Stronger incentives for producing high-quality science communication are also needed. Ensuring inclusive participation by diverse stakeholders is a pre-requisite for legitimate scientific debate and policy-making in a democratic society.

items.title: Environmental health resilience and exposure reduction for healthy aging and longevity.
items.abstract: Population aging has widened the gap between life expectancy and healthspan. Yet aging trajectories remain strikingly heterogeneous even among populations facing comparable harmful environmental exposures, including air pollution, extreme temperatures, toxic metals, unsafe water and sanitation, noise and poor housing. Why similar environmental risks produce divergent patterns of multimorbidity, disability and functional decline is a central research question. This Review proposes environmental health resilience factors, features of physical, social, ecological and built environments that act as protective effect modifiers, flattening the exposure-response curve and attenuating the biological translation of adverse exposures into harm rather than reducing exposure itself. Drawing on longitudinal cohorts, natural experiments and policy evaluations, we show that green and natural environments, age-friendly urban design, climate-resilient infrastructure and social connectivity flatten exposure-response curves and help to explain divergent aging trajectories under comparable urban environmental conditions. We propose both building resilience and reducing exposure are complementary strategies to compress morbidity and advance healthspan equity in aging societies.

items.title: Understanding the social determinants of healthy aging across the lifecourse with social policy experiments.
items.abstract: Social and economic conditions shape healthy aging, but it remains unclear whether policies that modify these conditions change aging-related biomarkers or later-life functional trajectories. The growing availability of biomarker data in longitudinal cohorts, together with the wider use of experimental and quasi-experimental designs in social policy research, creates new opportunities to evaluate how social conditions become biologically embedded. We argue that policy experiments can strengthen research on the biology of aging by specifying the exposure modified by policy, the populations affected and the life-course stage at which intervention occurs. Using education and cognitive aging as an example, and drawing on emerging evidence on policy effects on biomarkers, we show how causal evidence can diverge from observational associations. We propose a research agenda that integrates social policy evaluation with biomarker research, functional decline, resilience and healthy aging trajectories across the life course.

items.title: Personalised mobile health coaching from early pregnancy to 12-months postpartum for females at risk of gestational diabetes (Bump2Baby and Me): a multicentre, randomised controlled trial.
items.abstract: Maternal overweight and obesity increase the risk of gestational diabetes and adverse pregnancy outcomes. Digital health interventions offer scalable, personalised support, but evidence for interventions spanning both pregnancy and postpartum remains scarce. We evaluated the effectiveness of a personalised mobile health (mHealth) coaching intervention for females at increased risk of gestational diabetes. This multicentre, randomised controlled trial conducted in Australia, Ireland, Spain, and the UK enrolled pregnant females aged 18 years and older between 12-24 weeks of gestation with increased risk of gestational diabetes (Monash GDM risk tool score ≥3; tool risk factors were maternal age, BMI, ethnicity, family history of diabetes, and past history of gestational diabetes). Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) using computer-generated block randomisation (block size 200; stratified by site) to receive either personalised mHealth coaching via smartphone providing synchronous and asynchronous support through pregnancy to 12 months postpartum alongside usual maternity care, or usual maternity care alone. Usual maternity care, including gestational diabetes screening and management, continued unchanged in both groups, and both groups received Bluetooth-enabled scales. Participants and health coaches could not be masked to allocation; clinical staff providing usual care, laboratory staff, and trial statisticians were masked. The primary outcome was the between-group mean difference in BMI at 12 months postpartum among females at risk of gestational diabetes. The trial was registered at Australia and New Zealand Clinical Trials Register, ACTRN12620001240932. Between Feb 9, 2021, and Oct 22, 2023, 4386 females were screened, 3521 were excluded, and 865 were randomly assigned (437 to the mHealth intervention group and 428 to the control group). The mean age of participants was 35·2 years (SD 4·3), and most participants were White (588 [73%] of 804). Mean BMI change did not differ between groups (intervention, -0·04 kg/m2 [SE 0·12] vs control, 0·04 kg/m2 [0·13]). Adverse events were recorded in 18% (79 of 437) of participants in the intervention group and 25% (106 of 428) of participants in the control group; serious adverse events occurred in 6% (28 of 437) of participants in the intervention group and 9% (40 of 428) of participants in the control group. No adverse or serious adverse events were considered related to the intervention. Personalised mHealth coaching spanning pregnancy and an extended postpartum support period did not reduce mean maternal BMI at 12 months compared with usual care. Findings suggest that mHealth interventions targeting at-risk females might benefit from addressing a broader range of maternal health outcomes beyond weight management. items.title: Metal mixtures, industrial proximity, and child IQ: A cross-sectional biomarkers and longitudinal tooth analysis in schoolchildren from Taranto, Italy.
items.abstract: Children living near industrial sources may experience simultaneous exposure to multiple neurotoxic metals, with risks shaped by proximity, socioeconomic conditions, and developmental timing. We investigated associations among metal exposures, residential proximity to industrial sites and intelligence quotient (IQ) in 610 schoolchildren aged 6-15 years from Taranto, Italy. Child cognition was assessed using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, Fourth Edition ( WISC-IV) IQ and parental cognitive ability using Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices (SPM). Blood, hair, and urine biomarkers of cadmium, mercury, arsenic, lead, and manganese were analyzed cross-sectionally (n=437), while deciduous teeth reconstructed exposure across 22 time points (n=173). Analyses included regression, Spearman correlations, BKMR, BKMR-DLM, and TDLMM, adjusting for age, sex, SES, parental SPM, and proximity. Residence within 500m captured the strongest spatial signal for manganese and mercury. Urine cadmium (β=-3.12, p=0.001) and hair manganese (β=-0.0051, p=0.003) were inversely associated with IQ, and BKMR ranked cadmium as the dominant mixture contributor (PIP=0.98). Time-resolved models identified no robust metal-specific critical windows, while residence within 500m was consistently associated with lower IQ. Parental SPM was associated with child IQ and SES, while lower SES was associated with shorter residential distance from the industrial site. Near-source residence captured proximity-related metal elevations and cognitive disadvantage, while cadmium showed an IQ association without a clear spatial pattern. These findings highlight the sensitivity of metal-IQ associations to sample selection and covariate adjustment and underscore the importance of accounting for socioeconomic and residential factors when evaluating environmental metal exposures.

items.title: Ligand/receptor-based chimeric antigen receptors: a promising alternative to conventional scFv designs in cancer immunotherapy.
items.abstract: Engineering immune cells, particularly T lymphocytes, with chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) has become one of the most successful modalities of cancer immunotherapy, as evidenced by the approval and clinical use of multiple CAR-T cell products. Current CAR platforms predominantly rely on monoclonal antibody-derived single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) for target recognition. While scFv-based CARs have achieved remarkable clinical successes, they also exhibit notable limitations, including the potential to elicit anti-CAR immune responses, tonic signaling that contributes to CAR-T cell exhaustion, tumor escape via antigen loss or downregulation, and on-target, off-tumor toxicities. In response, researchers have explored alternative binding moieties for CAR architectures. Natural ligands and receptors represent one such class of alternatives. These approaches may offer advantages over conventional scFv-based CARs, such as potentially lower immunogenicity with fully human-derived domains, the ability to engage multiple targets or ligands, access to antigens that are challenging for scFvs, and the use of protein-protein interfaces shaped by evolution within human physiology. However, these benefits are not absolute. CAR junctions, non-native orientations, expression levels, modifications, and the cellular context can still generate immunogenic epitopes or dysfunctional products. Additionally, natural ligand/receptor pairs may transmit unwanted agonistic or regulatory signals that require careful engineering to mitigate. This review discusses recent advances in ligand/receptor-based CARs from a translational perspective. It also provides a critical overview of their inherent limitations, alongside potential solutions to support the rational design of next-generation constructs.

items.title: Health-related quality of life in early-stage type 2 diabetes: A cross-sectional study within the SMARTEST trial.
items.abstract: Normative health-related quality of life (HRQoL) data for people with early-stage, well-controlled type 2 diabetes are lacking. We aimed to describe the HRQoL profile of SMARTEST trial participants, contextualised against general population benchmarks. Baseline RAND-36 data (n = 1,501; domain scores range 0-100) were compared with population-based reference data using multiple linear regression adjusted for sex, age and education. Participants with 65 years, HRQoL exceeded reference population levels across several domains, particularly physical role functioning (β = 9.8, 95% CI 5.6; 13.9). Participants included during the pandemic reported a lower mental composite score (β = -2.5, 95% CI -4.5; -0.6). HRQoL in this early-stage type 2 diabetes cohort showed a distinct age-related pattern relative to general population benchmarks. Mental HRQoL during periods of societal disruptions merits further study.
